P RUDENTIAL ASSURANCE COMPANY, LIMITED.
CHIEF OFFICE: HOLBORN BARS. LONDON. SUMMARY OF THE REPORT PRESENTED AT THE FIFTIETH ANNUAL MEETING, HELD ON 2ND MARCH, 1899.

ORDINARY BRANCH—The number of Policies issued during the year was 64,708 assuring the sum of £6.420,580, and producing a New Annual Premium Income of £353.113. The Premiums received dvirinz the year were £2,987,501, being an increase of £193,237 over the Tear 1897. The Claims of the year amounted to £975,012. The number of deaths was 5,191 and 2,535 Endowment Assurances matured. The number of Policies in force at the end of the year was 534,138. INDUSTRIAL BR NCH.—The Premiums received during the year were £4,930,756 being an increase of £167,165. The Claims of the year amounted to £1.891,039. The num- ber of Deaths was 198,308 and 2,181 Endowment Assurances matured.

The numberef Free Policies granted during the year to those Policy-holders of five years' standing, who desire to dis- continue their payments, was 66.379, the number in force being 604,564. The number of Free Policies which became Claims during the year was 12,231. The total number of Policies in force at the end of the year was 12.99,679: their average duration exceeds eight and a half years. The Assets of the Company, in both branches ,as shevrn in the Balance Sheet, are £33,599,708, being an increase of £3.161,371 over those of 1897. Public attention having been for some time past directed to questions of thrift and provision for old age, the Dire2tors have had under consideration how they can further assist those Policy holders who from age and diminished earnings find some difficulty in maintaining the payment of Premiums on their Policies, and they have therefore made provision for all Policyholders in the Industrial Branch who have been assured for twenty-five years to be free from the payment of further Premiums as they attain the age of 75. This altera- tion takes effect at once, and has of course necessitated a considerable addition to the Reserves. .

div.p: LADIES' LETTER
111 Y DEAR NELLIE,

Spring is getting nearer and nearer and the general topic amongst ladies in regard to dress is the probability as to what character the spring costumes will take. If you will notice somo of the iashionable figures, however, you will soon get some idea or foreshadowings. A new industry, I notice, has almost been created in the matter of silk petticoats. What would our grandmothers have thought of these extravagant tastes, when they were content with simple tucked calico petti- coats for full dress occasions? Now the brocades, the glace silks, and the satins used for petticoats

are almost as elaborate as our dresses. The special fashions o• the in,»nent are brocaded skirts with a deep fl.,unce from the knee, composed either of alternate rows of white lace insertion and satin ribbon or a fancy kilted glace headed and edged by a ruche. Two examples of these are a hand- some white and petunia brocade, with white lace insertion and rich red mauve ribbon, and a light apple-green silk pcuit de sobs with the kilted flounces and ruche. Many rich black poult de soie petticoats have deep flounces treated with the6.l pipings or cordings, and they find great favaur in shirts. I will tell you as far as I can remember of a stylish jacket I saw which can be worn either opened or closed, and the collar will either stand up high round the throat, or roll back. This is made in cloth, in black, navy blue, dove-colour, fawn, or red, and the edges are braided with black and white silk braid. Toe revers and collar are faced with white moire; and the edges are braided to match the coat. Where jackets are worn they are mostly close fitting, and young girls will be wearing the waist jackets without doubt. The kilted silk chiffon, appears to form any

number of tuck:?, both in white and black, covers many of the revers and lines many of the collars. A great many grey jackets will be worn trimmed with white braid or appliqué bands; many of the revers are rolled back with acute points. The aleeves are severely simple, fitting the arm pretty closely at the base, but allowing sufficient fulness cm the shoulder for the epaulettes that appear on most of the dresses. A novel notion is the appli- cation of cloth to glace silk. This was exemplified in a triple cape of shot-green and fawn glac4 with lawn•coloured cloth stitched at the edge.

There are quite an extraordinary numb-er of fash- ionable etceteras and accessories without whilh at the present day, toilets are not considered at all finished. Jewellery, fans, feathers, and shoes all have their own particular style and variation' and one season the bow cannot be too fanciful for a shoe, whilst the following year a bow will be quite demode, and only a sparkling stud or a small flat tab fastened with a bucklc must appear. Other fancy adornments are high bands or slightly folded stocks of velvet are fashionable for evening wear, and these are decorated with crossed lines 4of pearls, with small paste buttons or stars set at

regular intervals all round, or to each edge is fas- tened a row of small pearls, and in the centre a star or a pendant, and on the left side is- a high band of velvet and on the left throe stars. A long rope of pearls is now worn, passing twico or thrice round the neck, and an aigrette of black velvet, a soupcon of lace, a star, and one upright feather, give the correct idea of this mode of adorning the coiffure. Powder puffq are very much In use now, and are made set artistically, and hidden so judiciously, that the owner can possess herself of it in a moment. They take the form of a little bunch of flowers that can be pinned on to the bodice, and are generally composed of violets, lilies-of-the-valley, or cowslips, surrounded by their own leaves.
Your loving JErmis.

High stiff col'ars are-liksly to disappear before long, which is an item to be thankful for, as it will thea be possible to uncover our necks and not be ashamed of them. The best frocks are be- ing built with a thin silk collar, round which lace, chif- fon, or lnightry-tinted silk may be lightly swathed. The best way to wash brushes is to dissolve a piece of soda the size of a walnut in a quart of hot water, and dip the bristles downwards into it, keeping the backs and handles as dry as possible. When clean, rinse the bristles in cold water. Wipe the backs and handles,but not the bristles which should be shaken and dried in the sun, or near a fire. Wining the bristles make them , soft, as does also the use of scap.

div.p: PAN MOBL.E,
"WOMEN'S CHAT."

Weather permitting, the Queen always brsaklasts out of &ors, at CiMIEZ, in the garden opposite her private apartments. This garden faces west and south, and while Her liljesty is seated there, she can enjoy the view of the Maritime Alps, or take in the encnanting panorama that ends in the distant ocean. Tea tao, the Sovereign delights in partaking of in the open air. During the afternoon drive, the Royal carriage i 4 fre- quently drawn up beneath the olives, at the roa side, where the meal is served, the servants and utensils hav- ing been sent on ahead. At the present time we are almost without Royalties. The Queen is at Cimiez, the Prince of Wales on the Riviera, the Princess ef Wales, Princess Charles of Den- mark,and Princess Victoria are cruising in the Medi- terranean, Princess Henry of Battenberg, the Duchess of York, and Princess Victoria of Schleswig-Holstein, are with Her Majesty, the Duke and Duchess of Connaught are still on the Continent, and the Duchess of Albany- has not yet returned from Germany. The only promi- nent member of the Royal Family who is at preFent within the four seas is the Duke of York. The children of the Duke and Duchess of York are re- maining quietly at Sandringham, where b.st part, of their day is spent in the open air. These little folks are very natural, and they are immense favourites with their numerous re'atives. They are always most simply dressed ; their little garments are made of the finest and rarest materials that money and good judgment can procure, but they are fashioned in a style peculiarly simple. The Rayal Family clings to the old-fashioned way of dre mine boys in skirts until they are four or five sears old, and as this example is generally followed British beys are condemned to skirts for a much longer pericd than their independent American-cousins. The marriage of Lord Crewe and Lady Margaret Primrose is fixed for the end.of next month, and pro- misee to b. as pretty a functien as it will be fashionable. The bride's eldest step-daughter elect is said to be de- lighted at the match, and will walk beside Lady Sybil Primrose in the bridal train. The Dowager Duchess of Cleveland, grandmother of tbe bride, who is expected to be present at the ceremony, is one of the most extraor- dinary old ladies now living, and quite the most remark- able lady member of our aristccracy. In her mind and manner she is not more than forty, and she is one of the inset amusing eonversationalists of which London Society can blast. Of late she has been entertaining a series of Saturday till Monday parties at Battle Abbey, her interesting old seat in Sussex, where sheZhas been residing since her return from the Riviera. We are now adopting another fashion set by our Parisienne sisters and this time the mode has good taste to forward its universal adoption. Women of hish de- gree in Paris seldom wear jewels for the church marri- age csremony, with the exception perhaps of a small string of pearls. Tte display of gigantic rubies,diamonds and other glittering ornaments in which Miss Vander- bilt appeared when she married the Duke of Marl- borough and the justifiable outcry which was raised about it at the time considerably helped to accelerate the departure of the old custom of piling on all one's jewels for the wedding ceremony. To us with our finey rooted idea that "happy is the bride the Fun shires on," it seems curious that a Breton bride should prefer to have a wet wedding, yet such is the case. It is held to signify that all her tears are now shed, and that she will therefore have a happy married life. The Errs of Bimbersk csll the day before the wed- ding the weeping dav,and the bride and her girl friends weep all they can. Some Greek tribes have a similar belief in the virtue of a drenching bringing good fortune and souse the bride with water. It has often been said that the stage as a profession, does not conduce towards long life,but the death of Mrs. Keeley—who had completed her ninety-third year—re- calls a list of actresses who lived to a ecod age. Helen Faucet was eeventv-nine when she died, Mrs. Sidden seventy-six,Kitty Clive seventy-four, Miss Sarah Thorne sixty-two,Mrs. Pritchard reached her fifty-seventh year, Mrs. Pope attained the same age, Mrs. Jordan was fifty- four at the time of her death, and Peg Weffingten was fifty-two. Madame de Navarre (Miss Mary Anderson) unlike ,he majority of actresses who have married, bas\no desire to return to the scenes of her former triumphs. She expresses her absolute dislike to the life of an actress, in the most decided way. Long before she had given up acting. she says, ehe had felt the hollowness of it all to the full. The glamour and glitter might please at first, but they could not satisfy for any length of time. First in Tunbridge Wells, and then in the charming Worcestestershire Tillage of Broadway—their present home—she and her husband have been supremely kbappp with th ir singing, music, picnics and country rambles, and later with their KM and heir. Madame ue Navarro is even more beautiful now than she was as Mary Ander- son. She seems to sweeten as she brcadens in her life, and motherhood, to her, is a veritable halo over her life. The woman who can dress with perfect Eimplicity,and yet challenge attendee in a crowd by reason of the faultless elegance of her appearance, has really achieved a triumph. Comparatively few persess tho secret. One of the few hew-ever is Geoneiana Countess of Dudley. On a recent oscaFicn she was immensely admired in the midst of gorgeously attired women, who seemed to vie with one another in eohibitine the brightest hues and most fisrnboyant fashions. Her costume was simplicity merzever, nets single strong color appeared in it. and the wearer looked like a delicate dower. Like the Princess of Wales she never forgets that dress should enhance, and be subordinate to the personal gifts of the wearer. Madame von And: e is another women who

_ invariably wears the right cictbes, and she has the adcii-I tioral alvantage of beautiful hair, which seems to arrange itself, 8) naturally does it fall into a graceful style. They spend very large sums in this way. Thirty peunds is a modest amount, while in rrany instances- £lOO is laid out in the course of a Tear. div.head: TETE EXAMINER FRIDAY, MARCH 17, 1899.
div.p: TETE EXAMINER FRIDAY, MARCH 17, 1899.
THE PEACE CRUSADE.'

div.head: MODIFICATION OF THE
div.p: A MODIFICATION OF THE
PILGRIMA.G-E.
THE NATIONAL CONVENTION.
BY W. T. STEAD.

With some measure of personal regret and dis- appointment, I make the announcement that the Pilgrimage of Peace has had to be abandoned in its original form for this year. The change, how- ever, is inevitable. Events have proved too strong to be resisted. There is no hope that the first pan of the Pilgrimage can be carried out; that the mission can be an expression of the real sentiment of the peoples represented upon it. Rather than diminish its ideal the committee has decided to forego, for the present year, the Pilgrimage as first conceived. _ _

•More • than two months have passed since the conception of the Pilgrimage of Peace was given to the world. Many things have happened in the interval. It may be well, therefore, to recall what it was that the Pilgrimage hoped to accom- plish. That will enable us the better to under-, stand why the idea of a great human snowball of Peace has had to be surrendered. First and foremost, the Pilgrimage was to be an expression of Anglo-Saxon unity. The nucleus about which the other nations would group themselves was to be a joint deputation representing England and the United States. Added to this were to be representa- tives of the seven smaller free States of Europe.

The ingimage. so constituted was to pass throtigh all the ....capitals of Europe, pleading the cause of peace and good-will among nations, gathering delegates at every halting-place, and finally arriving at St. Petersburg, bearing its message of 'hanks and encouragement to the throne of the,Czar. Such was the scheme, noble in its .simplicity and to all outward seeming easy of accomplishment. "Orom the first it took'hold of the imaginations of men. In Paris. and elsewhere on the Continent arrangements were made for the reception of the Pilgrims. A welcome worthy of the cause was promised. In various countries steps were taken for the appointment of delegates who should pro- ceed with the Pilgrims on their way to St. Peters- burg. From the first our Continental friend..; have laboured with an enthusiasm worthy of the highest praise. Theirs have been the chief diffi- culties. Here in England. we have had to deal with a people devoted to peace, and only await 7 the means to give expression to its sentiment. On the Continent there has been a long and unequal struggle against prejudice and against the ingrained traditions of generations. .

The lack of time has proved the chief eneiny of the Crusade. Probably no country in the world possesses so simple a means of voicing the'. opinion of the people as do' England. The calling of town's meetings is a process well understood. Englishmen are accustomed to give expression to their sentiments in public meetings. More than

two months have, however, bee ii spent in the organisation of England, which is a small country, while Scotland has scarcely yet commenced to make itself heard. If England has absorbed two months of ceaseless energy, it will be understood that more time is required for the Continent, and perhaps more still for that other vast Continent which it was hoped would take its place side •by side with England as banner-bearer of the Pilgrimage. Peace has had little consideration in America these months past: To rouse the whole of America from the Atlantic to the Pacific is at any time a work of superhuman difficulty. The obstacles presented by its huge geographical area are always there. These, however, were but the least of the obstructions to be overcome. The United States had when the Crusade commenced emerged recently from a great war in which its arms had proved triumphantly victorious. The whole country was rent with the disputes between the,„advocates and the opponents of expansion. It was hoped that this seething public opinion would soon settle down. Now, however, has arisen the trouble with the Philippines. Another session of Congress has been rendered necessary, and the hope of obtaining a delegation of senators, congressmen, and others has disappeared. There is no hope of an adequate American representation, therefore; and without this a main object of the Pilgrimage is impossible of accomolishmaT,E.

Tne impossibility of America joining adequately in the Pilgrimage is a set-back, but not the only one. On the Continent difficulties have arisen. Italy has taken up a strong attitude on the .ques- tion of the representation of the Pope at the International Conference. No objection would have been raised, in all probability, by the Italian Government had it not been for the ostentatious satisfaction of the representatives of the Pope at the recognition of his sovereignty. As it is, the dis- sensions in Italy make that country hopeless, for the time being, for the purposes of the Pilgrimage. In other directions other events have happened to disturb the arrangements. It has become known that in certain countries any attempt on the part of delegates to claim a national character will be met with determined opposition and agitation on the other side. The Continental Pilgrimage must necessarily, therefore, be inadequate, and it has been thought better to cut down the original

programme. Nobody has denied to the English portion of the Pilgrimage its right to claim that it represents the nation. The delegation will be elected at the National Convention, which will itself be a deputa- tion from the whole of Great Britain. Those who• will assemble on March 21st have been chosen at the series of town'sgmeetings all over the country. They include numerous members of Parliament, the Mayors of most el the great provincial towns, ministers of all &nominations, the chairmen of London Vestries, and all the representatives of a well-organised municipal life. Some idea of the truly representative character of the Convention can be obtained from the lists of delegates which are being published in War Against War. Con- servatives, Liberals, Socialists, and Labour will all be represented. No shade of political opinion or religious belief which has any claim to make itself heard will be excluded. A body of Pilgrims elected by such an assembly must be a microcosm of that great body of the nation which is in favour of an arrest of armaments. What is proposed is that the National Conven- tion shall choose the Pilgrims on March 21st. These will then set out on their mission to St. Petersburg. They will go straight to the capital of the Czar. England is the only country in which the national response to the Czar's Rescript has been adequate and unanimous. Great Britain in this matter occupies a unique position. Nowhere else is it possible to claim that any body of dele- gates will represent an opinion which has been expressed week after week, without faltering, throughout the length and breadth of the land. As Great Britain has occupied a unique position in the Crusade, so it will stand alone in the Pilgrimage. More than anything else we have to guard against any movement which can injure the Inter- national Conference at the Hague. If that assembly is to have any prabtical result its decisions must be absolutely unanimous. There is grave danger that were the Pilgrimage to go forward in the face of the feelings which have been aroused in certain countrieston the Continent injury rather than good would be done 'to he cause. Next year, however, an Apbstolate of Peace can have no diplomatic significance such as ;light now be attached to such; a mission. We go forward, then, looking to the future. In the spring of next year the Pilgrimage as first sketched may become an accomplished fact. There will be a great international conference at Paris at the time of the Exhibition, to promote the cause of the brotherhood of man. The work that has been done here and on the Continent will do much to further that congress. No effort that has been made will be wasted. The seed sown may not immediately spring into a ripe harvest, but sooner or later it will have its due fruition. The infancy of the twentieth century will see the reaping of the rich result of the work so laboriously done in the old age of the nineteenth.

div.p: (Copyright.)
PRINCESS DELILAH.

BY MRS. GEORGE CORBETT, Author of "Whan the Sea Gives up its Dead," "The Prince Physician," "The Vindication of Olive Trevethick, ' "The Star of Yukon," "The Adventures of an Ugly Girl," "Deb o' Aridly's," "A Fair Blockade Runner," eco.

CHAPTER XIX. A LOVER'S ERRAND. The Countess Sforza was entertaining a few select friends in her hired flat in Northumberland-avenue, ard among the guests were seyeral people whom we have met before. The Princiss Delilah, looking more royally beautiful than ever in a sweeping robe of white velvet, was the centre of attraction. ad the male guests nearly all vied with each other in bestowing upon her those attentions which women of her calibre regard as their just prerogative. Among her most devoted admirers was Mr. Price, the rich American, and he looked supremely happy, for, in common with all the men whom the Princess chose to enslave, 'he had been beguiled into thinking that he was the one upon whom the , siren intended to bestow her hand. There are some coquettes who urge their victims onwards by apparent coyness. But the Princess of Courland was not one of these. She preferred to let her lovers experience the intoxication of success, and not one of them but was willing to promise cautionsness when she told them that there were strong reasons why outsiders should not as yet know of "her engagement." Mr. Price was the most recent adherent to a long phalanx of ardent worshippers, and more than one person had already predicted that he would prove the successful suitor, for, although he *as no longer in his first youth, he was handsome, well- bred, and highly cultured, besides being rich enough to satisfy the caprices even of a Princess Delilah. He was about to join the lady who had won his affections, when the Countess, with whom he had just been talking, uttered a hurried exclamation of dismay. "0 Mr. Price," she cried, "something has happened to my ruby necklace! See, the clasp has broken, and if I had not been at home, I might easily have lost my most prized possession." "Do you really value it so highly as that ? " inquired Mr. Price, looking very pleased at the compliment he had received, for it was he who had presented the necklace to the Countess, on the occasion of her betrothal to his younger brother, whom a severe illness had carried off soon afterwards. It was certainly a very valuable gift, but the donor's instincts were as liberal as his wealth was immense, and it gladdened him to be told once more that his friend appreciated his offering for its personal associations more than for its pecuniary value. On examining the clasp, he was slightly puzzled to understand how it had managed to get broken, for it looked as if it had actually been cut with a sharp instrument, and, of course, such:a supposi- tion as that could hardly hold good. "We must hate the thing mended at once," said Mr. Price. "If you will trust me with it, Countess, I will take it to my hotel to-night, and will go to a jeweller's the first thing in the morning to get it mended; then you shall have it back withbut delay." "Thank you, Mr. Price. You are always kind to me." Thus said the Countess, and she had no mis- givings about the safety of her property when she saw her old friend put it into his pocket, having first wrapped it carefully in a silk pocket-handker- chief, in lieu of the velvet-lined case in which it was kept when not in use. "There now," he observed," it will be just as safe there as in the case, and it won't take up so much room." • "Mind you don't get your pocket picked on your way home," said the Countess laughingly. "Trust me for that," was the equally smiling reply, neither of the talkers having noticed that the whole proceeding had been attentively watched by one of the guests. At this moment the Duke of Hapsburg-Solltesein claimed the attention of the pretty little Countess, and Mr. Price once more sought the side of Princess Delilah, who welcomed him with a kindli- ness of manner which set the blood tingling in his veins with delighted excitement. Lady Flora Vavasour-Pomeroy was also present, and the Princess was not so engrossed with Mr. Price's conversation that she was unable to be keenly observant of every other person in the room. She saw that Lady Flora was fair enough to tempt any man's heart frem him, and her blue eyes looked on in half contemptuous amusement while Prince Carlos fluttered about his divinity like a moth hovers over a candle. "Carlos has really lost his heart this time, and I must warn him to beware lest he allows himself to be led into jeopardising our joint interests. It will never' do for him to marry, for in that case our partnership would have to come to an end, unless the Duke and-I were also willing to entrust our safety to the keeping of a person who might be afflicted with such an uncomfortable thing as a conscience. On the other hand, Lady Flora is in too high a social position, ,and is too well sur- rounded by friends, for any man to bring about a public coupling of her name with his without being ' duly punished if his addresses do not terminate honourably."' This was the burden of the Princess Delilah's thoughts the while she exchanged society chit-chat with Mr. Price, who was so delighted by her evident preference for his company that he had neither eyes nor ears for anyone else in the room. Nor was it until some time after the entrance of the Duke of Hapsburg-Solltesein that the Princess began to find the American millionaire's attentions irksome • and as soon as she realised her state of mind, she smilingly ended her tete-a-tete with him by rising from her seat with the remark: "We can have another chat presently, Mr. Price. Just now,l feel that I owe some little attention to our hostess, who informed me in a note that she had something very particular to say to me." Mr. Price's fair cheeks flushed with disappoint- ment, but he had no choice except to make the best of the situation, and he bowed courteously as the Princess Delilah left him, to walk gracefully up the room towards where the Countess Sforza was allowing herself a little remission from the duties of the evening. But it was not for the sake of hearing anything particular from the pretty lips of her hostess that the Princess Delilah joined 'her. She was actuated by a far different motive, and although her face was as smiling as ever, she had been filled with sudden rage at sight of the evident admiration which shone from the eyes of the Duke of Solltesein. "Great Heaven! " was her mental ejaculation. "Is it possible that Otto is actually falling in love? I have heard him boast scores of times that he was proof against woman's wiles, and that he scorned to yield to the passions which helped him to govern other men. But I know the symptoms too well to mistake them, and I will crush any woman who dares to pose as my rival." "How very beautiful the Princess is to-night!" was the remark made by Lady Flora to Prince Carlos, and the latter glanced arelessly in the direction indicated by his pretty charmer's eyes. His carelessness, however, gave place to inward concern, for he also was a skilled student of physiognomy, and he knew how to interpret the expression on the Princess Delilah's face, in spite of its mask of amiability. "The mischief t" he thought. "She is becoming suspicious, and the deuce knows what will happen if a woman like that grows jealous! I must warn Otto not to make such a fool of himself, if he doesn't want to ruin us." It will be easily gathered from all this that the Duke, the Prince, and the Princess, all three of them !seine people ivho needed to keep their wits unclouded', were shewing themselves to be as pervious to the universal passion as the most simple creature alive. Not that the fact of being in love is an. inevitable corollary of simple-mindedness. But from Antony and Cleopatra downwards it has long been noticed that great schemers degenerate in their scheming when they fall under the dominion of Cupid, for the head and the heart are hereditarily antagonistic, and there was just reason for the dismay which was felt by Prince Carlos, although he might fairly well have coupled himself with du Duke when he alluded to him as a fool. But Cupid had not as yet so fully conquered the trio as to rob them of all ambition and enterprise, and the Princess Delilah knew very well why and whither her two friends took their departure quite early in the evening, after duly excusing them- selves to the Countess. The former was still inwardly fuming with jealous resentment, and if some of the people with whom she laughed and chatted could have gauged the real drift of her thoughts, they woia havo reeoal64 fY9,in her in agt_Quialied dismay.

Meanwhile Mr. Price recovered his cheerful- ness for thp bpAutiful Princess condescended to be inore gracious than ever, and her fascinations we e so potent that he would have gone to the end of the world for her if she had asked him to do so. He was, therefore, a very good subject for the experiment she wished to make. "Now then, Mr. Price," she said, her very voice 'seeming to be more melodious than that of any other woman, while she spoke so low that no one but he could distinguish what she said, "now then, Mr. Price, you profess to be very fond of me---" "As I live," he interrupted, "I love you so madly that I would give up the whole world for your sake!" "Foolish creature! I do not want you to give up anything for my sake; and I cannot tell you how happy I am to have won the regard of so true a man as you are. There is no need for you to prove your love, for my heart responds to it; and no man has ever before been able to move me as you do! :`cro, don't get excited or you will attract attentim, and I want: you to do me a small service without •tvovone noticing it:" One small service!" was the reply. "A. 5,1 r.,-,zousand of me and I shall be only too happy to obey you!" "You have heard—but no you will only laugh at for what I am about to ask you may strike you as very silly." "Nothing you could do or say would be 51137; and I am waiting to do your commands." "Very well. You have heard of Madame Celia, the clairvoyante and fortune-teller ? "
!!Have you ever seen her?"

"Not yet." "Nor have I. But lam very anxious to consult her at the earliest opportunity, ; and I want you to call at her house—l will give you the address presently—and make an appointment with her for me. I should like to see her to-morrow, if possible,- and I shall be immensely, obliged to you if you will arrange the affair for me without letting anybody else know anything about it." Mr. Price smiled indulgently, and at once rose to his feet, saying softly: "I hate to leave you; but lam delighted to do you a service; and as soon as you give me the address you spoke of, I will try to find the wonderful clairvoyante, of whom I have already heard a great deal." "Here is the address," returned the Princess, almost inaudibly. "You will find the place with ease. But remember my caution: do not let any- body know where you are going." "And when shall I see you again ? " was the eager inquiry, to which the answer was: "As a rule, I never receive even my lady friends before twelve o'clock, but I will make an exception in your favour, and if you care to come to me, I will await you at ten o'clock to-morrow morning." The Countess Sfor•za was very much disappointed to lose another of her guests, especially one with whom she was on terms of comparative intimacy; but Mr. Price excused himself so skilfully that she pardoned his defection, and he emerged into the street without anyone but the Princess Delilah having the least idea that he was not going straight home.

div.head: CHAPTER XX.
div.p: CHAPTER XX.
WHAT IS PRINCESS DELILAH?

Mr. Price drove as far as Leicester-square in a hansom which, mindful of his promise of secrecy, he dismissed opposite the Empire Theatre • and the cabman, if he thought of his fare at all, merely thought that he had come too late to see much of the show. _

But as soon as the infatuated lover saw himself unobserved, he quietly walked a little further, and very readily found the address he sought. As had been the case with Lord Alfred and his companions, there were few obstacles in the way of obtaining admission to the house; but as he bad no previous appointment, he was asked to wait downstairs until madame's attendant could bring him a reply to his note. He did not expect this reply to be delayed many minutes, but he was kept waiting for -what seemed to him quite an uncon- scionable time; and he was both surprised and impatient at so unbusinesslike a proceeding. When at last his impatience would no longer be controlled, he rose from the seat whereon he had been sitting, and touched a gong which caused the attendant to present himself immediately. "Did you wish for anything, sir ? " was the question. "Certainly! I want a reply to my note. Have you given it to your mistress ? " "Yes, sir; and she bade me say to you that she would receive you herself very shortly. I daresay she is ready now; and if you will kindly wait five minutes more, I will conduct• you to her. Ah! there goes her bell, and there is no need to wait any longer. Will you please follow me upstairs ? " Mr. Price had heard a great deal concerning the marvellous powers of the clairvoyants, whose reputation as a mystic was very much enhanced by the fact that she declined any overtures of further acquaintanceship, and accepted none of the invita- tions which were sometimes sent to her by enterprising hostesses who desired to secure a great attraction without having to pay too much for it. His curiosity was, therefore, already strongly aroused,; and he stepped eagerly into the gloomy presence-chamber, expecting to see Madame Celia at once. But another disappointment awaited him, for she was not there, though the Oriental servant, after asking him to be seated, assured him that she would be with him in another moment: The moment proved a long one; and his impatience was already returning, when he detected a curious odour, which instantly put him on the alert, for it was always associated in his mind with danger. "Chloroform!" he thought. "What can be the meaning of that ? Is it possible that there is trickery at work here, and that there is to be an attempt to rob me? If so, they shall find me a tough customer to deal. with!" Even as the American thought this, he rose softly to his feet, and turned round just in time to stop an attendant from pressing a handkerchief over his face. This handkerchief was -Saturate d with chloroform; and but for Mr. Price's phenomenally keen scent, he would have been overpowered and rendered unconscious before he could have risen to defend himself, for there had not been the slightest noise to indicate that he was no longer alone in the room. - - -

"You dog! " he exclaimed, as by an unexpected move he snatched the handkerchief out of the Oriental's hand, only to have it taken from him in turn by a second Oriental, who had evidently been stationed ready to enter the room, in case his accomplice should need his help. But they had reckoned without their host, if they thought to conquer Mr. Price easily, for he was as strong as either of them, and he was not the sort of man to lose his life through faintheartedness. pike a flash, he aimed a furious blow at the head of his first assailant, and the man staggered back under the force of the onslaught. But his companion saw his chance and had almost succeeded in applying the death-dealing handker- chief, when he also felt the weight of Mr. Price's fist.

With low cries of rage, both the men drew out their long, murderous-looking knives, and their intended victim, seeing that it was really a matter of his life or theirs, felled one of them with a terrific blow on the temple, springing aside just in time to avoid being stabbed by assassin Number Two. • Without a ,groan; the first man rolled over, stunned and unconscious; but the other man, warned by his companion's fate, jumped and dodged about lust out of reach of the American's formida,ble fist, all the while watching his chance of driving his knife .home, Once, twice, thrice he managed to inflict slight wounds in the arm; and Mr. Price was covered with blood ere' he succeeded in landing a blow which sent 'his antagonist reeling backwards: To follow up his hard-won advantage was the work of a moment, anti? he positively rained blows upon the man: ThetMe stood panting, perspiring, bleeding, and well-nigh exhausted, but, nevertheless victorious, though his heart quailed for a 'moment when he saw that both the villains lay senseless on the floor. "Good Heavens!" he ' thought. "What have I done? If r have killed these scoundrels, my life is in danger, for I should, perhaps, never be able to prove that I was acting in self-defence when I struck them. Surely they are not both dead!" Kneeling down, the victor looked anxiously for traces of animation in his cowardly asiailants, anei soon satisfied himself that they were both still alive, although they were losing blood rapidly—fe: one of them had fallen on his knife, and the °dux had been 0) badly punished that he bled copiously,. M. Price boasted a rough-and-ready knowledge surgery among his numerous accomplishments; and, hastily tearing their scarves into strips, he tightly bandaged the Wounds, so as to stop the bleeding. "The rascals will need better treatment later on," was his hurried reflection, "for if their injuries don't prove fatal in the long run, they are sure to leave permanent mischief behind them. gsit it
vttLl not
leg. ee t any precaution

against, prcvoo.:•!,, ; and before 1 40 for help, I ••• illipoSsible for them IA " 1 He found plenty of material close at hand to suit his purpose, and soon had both men so well. gagged and bound, that, although by this time, their scattered senses had returned to them, theil were quite unable to do anything towards extrica-i ting themselves from the unpleasant position in' which they were placed. All this time Mr. Price had been working with feverish energy, hardly recognising the real peril of his situation, now that he had assured himself that the injuries he had inflicted upon the two treacherous Orientals werø. not fatal. 11F- lair •

Suppose the police, scenting something unusua., were to force an entrance into the house, it would be difficult to imagine a more compromising, position than he would be in. He was in a strange house, at a late hour of tbe! night, and-it would be necessary to prove that he had come upon a legitimate errand, instead of asi a thief who had wounded, gagged, and bound the' two servants of the house who had presumably": attacked him in defence of their mistress's pro.‘, perty. Instead of at once making his escape, ag many men would have done, he was seized with io burning desire to learn as much as he could about the House of Mystery which he had entered ag unsuspectingly as a child, and, fight against the; conviction as he would, he could not help wonderi ing if the object of his recently awakened love had known more of this place than she professed ta know when she sent him thither. _ _

Of course, it might turn out that there was nothing in it. But, upon mature reflection, there certainly seemed no reason why he should have been asked to come here so secretly, and at such al, unseasonable time. The Madame Celia to whom he had brought the Princess Delilah's note had as yet given no sign of her presence; and it was quite safe to assume that she was not in the house, or Oa would surely have been either seen or heard after the commotion which had been made during the fight. If she was not really here, why did her servant pretend that she would see the caller in a fevO. minutes, unless the• whole attack had been pre° arranged? And how was it that this attempt upon his life had been made at the very time when he was in possession of the Countess Sforza's necklace He had been very remiss in forgetting all about it when he sallied out on the Princess Delilah's, errand; and he hastily put his hand into his inner coat pocket to assure himself that the treasure waS still safe. It certainly was where he had put it ; but the fact only served to make his situation morel compromising in the event of premature discovery, for it would bear out the very natural theory that he was here on a burglarious errand, in spite of his gentlemanly manners and appearance. Nevertheless, he was reluctant to forego his chance of probing the mystery to the bottom; and he looked round irt search of the note which he had carried hither, aS, a perusal of it would at once and for ever set hill mind at rest concerning the purport of the naessaga which the treacherous Arabs had interpreted ixt such an extraordinary manner; but it was nowher- in the presence-chamber, unless it was in thyl pocket of one of the vanquished men. He soo satisfied himself on this score, and then searche. the apartment downstairs with equal non-success. Returning to the first floor, he unhesitatingly pushed aside a heavy portiere, and passed into IS smaller room, which was en suite with the presence°, chamber, and which had another door communics4 Ling with the staircase. This door was locked fro:, the inside, so it was quite evident that no one hail, left the room unknown to Mr. Price since he cam; upstairs, unless the presence-chamber itself wag used for the purpose, for the inner apartment wait' nothing but a well-furnished dressing-rooms evidently intended for the use of a lady. Silver backed brushes, ivory combs, and crystal scent bottles abounded, everything being indicative of th owner's luxurious tastes. There is sometimes no accounting for men • vagaries, and Mr. Price was astonished at himse for permitting doubts of the Princess Delilah ' torture him. Yet so it was, and it was with con stantly augmenting anxiety that he hunted for iii means of setting his mind at rest. Eventually li. found what he sought, and withdrew from unclo. the dressing-glass an envelope addressed in th• Princess Delilah's handwriting, which he recognise.' as the one which she had given to him s reptitiously earlier in the evening. "Now I shall know what my beautiful darlin. said," was the tormented lover's joyful reflectio "I must be mad to allow myself to doubt her for moment, and I cannot understand how su ' preposterous ideas have got into my head." Mr. Price felt positively angry with himself fo his want of faith. But his anger changed in another channel after he read the note which h had sought so anxiously. "I send you a friend; treat him carefully," h' read. "Your reward, as usual, will be accordin: to your success." There was not another word more, but there Iv quite enough to make Mr. Price reel with Budd,' horror, for in the light of subsequent events, h• could only give one interpretation to the bri• message. Certainly, to an outsider, there nothing compromising in the letter, for it was fai spoken enough, and was just the sort of epistle ths a woman of Madame Celia's profession migh expect to receive from a client or a friend wile understood her peculiarities. But Mr. Price did not think there was anythi: vague about it. The Princess Delilah had profess to be anxious to consult the clairvoyants for the time; had said that she had never seen her; an. had sent hither a man who carried in his pocket valuable necklace, and who, in conformity with 13( wishes, had carefully concealed his mission fro) anybody else. All this pointed to deliberate, fel design, and though his brain reeled with horrifiel amazement, the man who had so nearly fallen victim to deep-dyed treachery found himself utterl unable to reconcile existing facts with his ow hopes of exonerating the Princess Delilah from knowledge of the affair. "Your reward, as usual, will be according your success." Those words were in themselves a proof that tb! writer of them was often in communication NVii, the person to whom they were written. Yet thoug', Mr. Price was nearly demented with the shock a maddening conviction, he sought for some proof t: there might be a mistake, after all, and hesitat, only a few seconds to open a small box whia formed part of the furnishing of the large dressinf table. The sight of its contents would have been re( of a revelation to Lord Alfred and others than was tolaim for they would have known what think of the long coils of purple-black hair whii were attached to a woman's wig, and of the won& fully-made waxen mask which, in conjunction the wig, was capable of transforming any of similar build into a perfect presentment of t"' much talked of clairvojante, Madame Celia. "An impostor! Madame Celia is an impostal But—what is Princess Delilah ? " Such was the question the unhappy man as, himself, even as a light footfall sounded bebi him, and a voice cried in accents of the intense relief: "Thank Heaven that I find you safe! Oh, - dearest, you don't know how anxious I have been Then a woman's arms clasped his neck; woman's kisses were -rained upon his cheeks ' lips; and in spite of the doubts ,and fears of night, one glance into the matchless blue eyes the Princess Delilah won back his faith in her. (To be continued.)

TROUBLES.
SURPRISING CURE AT STOCKPORT.
A repc-r-te-; of the "The Cheshire Daily Echo" has been furnished with a striking testimony by Mr. Henry Hall, of 62, Wood-street, King-street West, 80uthp3rt.

Mr. Hall said, "Two years ago I was first seized with a strange nervous attack: my whole system was agitated ;my limbs were altermately drawn and expanded utterly against my will, and I was simply paralysed. By a doctor's instructions I was taken to the hospital, but was eventually discharged, little better. I was placed on the outdoor list, but 1 grew worse; the attacks sometimes occurred three or four times a week, and in- creased in violence. I was unable to follow my employ- ment."

Mrs. Hall interposed. "We had read of Dr. Williams' Pink Pills for Pale People in the papers. and my husband was recommended to use the pills by a railway porter in Heaton Norris, who assured him of the good he had per- sonally received from their use. It was with very little hope that I got the first box; in fact, he had taken three boxes before I began to see that they were doing him good. At the end of the third box he would have given the gills up, but I saw evidences of his improvement, and urged him to continue their use. Graivally the fits loFcame less frequent and very much less violent, and now, as you see, my husband is altogether a new man. We are amply rewarded for our trouble, I can assure you.,,
A LIFE SATED AT BELFAST.

Recently there came under my notice, writes a re- porter of "The Belfast Weekly News," the case of a young married woman, Mrs. Isabella Curry, 58, Louisa- street, Belfast, whose story is as follows :—Six months

ago I commenced spitting up blood, and.as it continued I went to the dispensary and got a bottle of medicine, but the flow of blood increasing, I became alarmed, and went to a doctor, who gave me some medicine to stop the bleeding. He said it arose from an ulcer in the stomach.

"The medicine," continued Mrs. Curry, "did not do me the slightest apparent good. The flow of blood be- came worse, and was accompanied by a cough. My appetite left me, and I became so weak I could neither eat nor sleep. Becoming morealarmed at my condition, I went to another docter. I was in bed for two weeks. My husband's friends had given up all hopes. They thought that I had but a very short time to live. _ _

•• I had been suffering for over six weeks, when one of the little bpoks sent out by Dr. Williams' Medicine Company was left at my house. I sent for a box of Dr. Williams' Pink Pills, and after taking them for three or four days I felt benefitted and was able to eat and sleep. I continued to take the the pills, and am now as *ell as ever I was. Dr. Williams' Pink Pills saved my life, and I believe if it had not been for them I would have been dead long ago. I can now eat and sleep wellr and am in the best of health."

div.head: FENELLA. DISASTER.
div.p: THE FENELLA. DISASTER.
FUNERAL OF MR. J. F. WHITE.

The inquest on the body of Mr. .T.F.White was held at Fleetwood Police Station on Friday evening, last week. Mr. F. R. Roberts, seiicitor, Warrington, appeared for the relatives of the deceased. The jury returned a ver- dict that the deceased was washed overboard, and accidentally drowned, and added a rider that the Steam Packet Company should exercise more authority in com- pelling passengers to go below. The b ,dy of the late Mr. James Frederick White was removed from _the Fleet woad mortuary to the railway station, and was conveyed by passeager train to War- rington on Friday night last, where it was met by several relatives and friends. It was then transferred to a hearse and taken to the Cemetery chapel, where it remained until the funeral, which took place at two o'clock on Saturday afternoon. Th 3 first part of the service was conducted in he chapel, by the Rev. William Potts, superintend eat of the Warrineton Wes- leyan Circuit. The chief mourners were Mr. James White (father),Messrs. George,Frank,and Ernest Whits, (brothers), W. White (uncle), Mr. Stephen Dale (father- in-law), Mr. J. C. Heckle, Mr. Donald Dale (bro:her-in- law), Mr. Edward Heckle, and other. At the close ot the service in the chapel the rev, gentleman said the memory of their dear brather had been cherished by the Wesleyan body in Padgate and Warrington, yet they dad not think of him as persons without hope. ,He was at the present time before Christ, which was far better. There was a sense of satisfaction that the mem- bers of the bereaved family were thus enabled to follow ti the grave the one they loved. The body was barna from the sanctuary to the grave on the shoulders of six of the deceased gentleman's intimate friends, viz:—Messrs. T H Granger, Thomas S Steel(who were associated with Mr White for nix years whilst in the office of Mr W H J Jenkins, solicitor). Henry Taylor, Walter Ashton, William Dakin, and Arthur Taylor. At the graareside several hundreds of persms had assembled, and amongst those present were Wain. Councillors Arthur Bennett and F It Roberts, W H J Jenkins, George Clay and J Proctor Jones (Mersey Beistaad Com- pany), Frederick Taylor, F Wright ad H Ward (super. intendants of the Padgate Wesleyan Sunday School, of which the deceased had bsen hart. secretary for several years), F E Taylor, S B Stringer, E S Garland.o Barton, Ernest Andrews, G H W Steel, E L Peareo,J Harrington, Arthur Ward, S Dawson, G James, .Tames Ford. W Pearce, Dyson Whitham, Csrruthers, E Steel, Dixon (Manchester-road), George Clay, Walter Clay, Mr Mills, and other representatives from the Mersei Bed- stead Company. the Y.M.C.A., and the Arpley Lawn Tennis Club. At the grave the service was impressively conducted by the Rev. W. Potts, many of those oreaeot being visibly affected. There were a large number of floral tributes, including " A tribute of sorrow from his grief-stricken widow," his father and mother, his sister and brothers, Mr and Mrs Stephen Dale and family, the officers and teachers of the Padgate Wesleyan Sunday School, the directors of the Mersey Bedstead Company, the Arpley Lawn Tennis Club,Mr and Mrs William Ben- nett and family. Mr J C Heckle. Mr and Mrs Dean, Mr T H Granger,Par and Mrs F R Roberts. the staff of .Messrs Thewlis and Griffiths, Limited, [Mr Charles B Smith, Mr and Mrs HR Ezard. Mr William Dskih, Mr and Mrs Everett and family, Mr and Mrs Unsworth4and Mr Thomas S Steel.

WARRINGTON VOLUNTEER'S EXPERIENCE OF ECZEMA,
At 6, General-street, Warrington, resides Mr. George Ryder, a volunteer sergeant, much respected in the War- rington battalion. His occupation is that of a horse

shunter on the aailway, and about five years arto,shortly after rubbing down a horse suffering from scrofula. he noticed a" breaking out," as he termed it to a local re- porter, on both his bands. Local medical men were con- sulted, who diagnosed his complaint as eczema. Various remedies were tried, but he was compelled to obtain other ad.vice, and for seven weeks was a patient in the Manchester and Salford Hospital. He had no sooner returned to wok than the disease broke out again with renewed vi,gour,and he had to go about with both hands, very much swollen, wrapp-d up in cotton gloves. o,:casionally the flesh was torn off his hands when he removed the bandages, and his condition was pitiable in the extreme. A. specialist was now consul- ted, but still the pain aid trouble continued.

• At length:be:heard of a similar skin diseasebeingcured by Dr. Williams' Pink Pills for Pale People. He obtained a box of the pills, and when the contents of the second box had been taken he noticed a great improvement in his hands. After a fcurth box was takon he no longer had occasion to go to work with covered hands, and he informsd the reporter that he regards Dr. Williams as a public banefactor. He is in excellent bodily health, and no one could tell from an examination of his hands that he had so long suffered from such a troublesome disease.

div.head: AMR, TEE WAR,
div.p: AMR, TEE WAR,
Br MR. H. WIIITHIM.

The United States Government is now having such an experience as it has not had before. Hitherto it-has been able to watch with the utmost complacency the doings of European Governments. To act the critic has been easy work, and so long as the trouble kept outside, the United States could always be accompanied with a lot of self-satisfac- tion. All this is now altered, the war with Spain over, and the Don humbled to the dust, the Ameri- can people are just a little puzzled what to do with the flotsam they find on their hands. It is a differ- ent question to settle. From the Atlantic to the Pactfic are States whose interest in the question of retaining the Paillipines are very varied, and it seems to be .almost impossible to bring abbe a settlement from an altruistic point of view. The Western press urge, almost unanimously, the re- tention of the islands, either as Territories, or, what seems the much more difficult plan, the annexa- tion and the building up of a new State; The latter mode of settling the trouble is difficult, for various reasons The writers of the American consqtution could not foresee the thousand and one contingencies that were likely to arise ere the bebe, at whose birth they were assisting, should arrive at matu- rity. Hence it happens to-day that the constitu- tion, and the wishes of the people are somewhat in conflict. alore than this, as I have stated, the People are divided in opinion as to what had best , be done in the matter. In the West here, the ques- tion is lookel at from a purely business standpoint. It is urged that the retention of the Phillipines would mean a rrreat increase in the trade of the Pacific slope, Day after day the Repubriean press manage to unearth fresh trade features whereby San Francisco is to be especially benefited by the retention of these far away islands. The Democra- tic press in its turn does all it can to belittle these Imperialistic teachings, In a number of the Eastern states a different policy is pursued. It is more in accordance with the feeling held by the great masses of the people before the war, and it is still more in line with the just Republican traditions held dear by all who are at all acquainted with American history. The resolution offered by Senator Hoar to the Senate at Washington covers the Anti-Imperialistic ground and I cannot do better than give it. It reads as follows :—" Resolved, that the people of the Philippine islands of r;ght ought to b' free and independent ;that they are absolved from all allegi- ance to the Spanish crown and that all the political connection between them and Spain is and ought to he totally dissolved, and they have, therefore, full power to do all acts and things which independent states may of right do; that it is their right to in- stitute a new government for themselves, laying a foundation on such principles and organising its power in such form as to them shall seem most likely to effect their safety and happiness and that with these rights the people of the United States do not propose to interfere." There is no doubt in my mind that the war,with Spain and the crushing defeat she met with at the hands of Uncle Sam has had a most demoralizing effect on the people. It has brought about a dream of imperialism, and we know what such dreams meanlin tax-ridden Europe. In the words of Kipling we learn the cost— "We have fed our se % for a thousand years, And she calls us still unfed, Though there s never a wave of all her waves But marks our English dead. We've chewed our best to the weed's unrest, To the shark and the sheering gull ; If bloxl be the price of admiralty Lord God; we have paid it in full." - Justice Brewer once said, "Infinitely stronger for

the cause of freedom then the power of our armies is the force of our example," and it is this force of example that the best brains, and the purest minis of America have been E4CI proud of; have written so lovingly of ; that is now abant to be thrown to the wind-. Bat what is it all about? For quite a number of years the civilized world has been looking for, nay, has been expecting with a feverish anxiet.y.the most fearful war the world ever saw, and still it conies not. Every little while we seem to be just on the verge of it. The nations of Europe look on with jealousy when Ameriea carries her victorious navy from Cuba to the Philipines. The Garman admiral of tee squadron in Manila Bay wked the British Admiral what he (the British Admiral) would do if the Germans opened fire on Dewey's fleet. The British Admiral's reply ii re- ported to have been "Admiral Dewey and myself are the only ones who know." Thus it is seen, the expected conflagration was very near to us. Again in the Fashola incident were we treadin.g perilously near the dreaded outburst. In Eastern Europe the complaint seems to be chronic in spite of all the peaceful pretensions of the Auto- crat of all the Russias. Again we may ask, what is it all about? The answer is a long and tedious one, and at the risk of somewhat boring my readers I may be excused if 1 give ray version of it. I might answer in litief,that it is the extreme anxiety of each nation's Government to provide sufli3ient employment for its own people. America, for instance. now makes the announcement that she can produce as mach in seven months as she can • eensume in twelve months. So she, like the rest of the nations feels the feverish excitement, and looks around for a way out of the coming trouble. It is an unmistakable fact that we are stupidly closing our eyes to the fierce and merciless in lus- trial and the commercial rivalry that is growing up around us. We think to down it by increasing our armies and navies, and fighting for each new market as it Comes to the front. The greater development of all the moral and na- tural forces; the increased, and steadily increasing productive power of machinery, the better organ- ization of labour and its insistence upon a larger share of life's comforts, mean something more than a mere" living wage" to the worker. They mean first, that foreign markets must be found, hence the growing armies and navies. They mean, again, that the potential power of a nation, its developed and undeveloped power, as an industrial arid com- mercial natioa,will be that n ations measurement of strength among the nations of the earth. We may now ask in all seriousness is civilisation the success it is said to be? Might is now right, and we seize the lands of the weak so that we may give bread to the congested populations of our cities. it is cal- culated that the population of the Uuited States will at the end of the twentieth century number 1,280,000,000, with certain Qualifications, the popu • lation of Europe will have similar increase, so we arrive logically, at the conclusion, that if no fresh markets are found, it will very son cease to be a question of eight hours a day, and increase in consumption will have to go hand in hand with in- crease in production, or four hours a day will settle the business. Here we are face to face with the real cause of all the disturbance. Until now the European: and American labourers have not been placed in comparision with the Asiatic labeurer. In America laws have been repeatedly passed for the purpose of keeping out the Chinase, and to a cer- tain extent. the Jape. These laws have been more or less a failure. Laws are in existence forbidding labor contracts, having slavish tendencies in them, from being carried out. Hawaii, a recent ac- quisition of the States, abounds with this kind of labour, and all the efforts GE. the friends of labour at Washington to put a stop to it are failures. The capitalist demands cheap labour, hence his indiffer- ence to the demands of labour. it is the dread of

this7cheap labour that is now causing so much. anxiety in labour ranks touching the annexation or retention of the Phillipines. It is plainly seen teat teese islands may act as a bridge over which the Asiatic may find his way to the States I have given pretty close attention to the Asiatic and his ways. To the writer and the speaker deal- ing with the subject I always pay attention. and I am bound to endorse the general view taken by these observers of the Chinaman. According to all appearances China is likely, in the near future, to be divided up between the leading powers. This I look upon as the beginning of the greatest revolu- tion the labour world ever saw, and it cannot be too strongly insisted upon that the words of Thorold Rogers shall be adopted as the motto of all workers. "Employers will get labour as cheap as they can. It is the business of the State to prevent them get- ting it so cheaply that they imperil the future of the race by the process." The determination to get this cheap labour is now proclaimed, and I quote from a recent issue of the "Iron Trade Review," published atteleveland, Ohici —"The impatient,sometimes sneering, 'ls this pros- perity?' which accompanies newspaper announce- ments of reductions in wages, indicates that there are many who utterly fail to ap- preciate the conditions under which pros- perity, of whatever proportions it may prove to be, will come to this country. Wage reductions are certainly a feature ofthe new prosperity. The scale of profits is gone. The basis of values is often treated as temporary and transitional. That is a characteristic which promises to stay until industrial capital and labour get used to it. An element that may be reasonably looked for in the prosperity to come is larger tonnage, much of it gained in foreign trade, which can only be had through lower prices and lower wages. The pros- perity of the future will Consist in having much to do rather than in having large profits and high wages."ln plain English this means that prosperity in protected America will be more labor for less money, that the" pauper labor "of Europe is to be met', in America by longer hours, and less wages. A cheering outlook this, considered from my point of view, as I seldom leave work Saturday evenings be- fore seven or eight O'clock, and it is often nine or ten. This is where the Asiatic gets on at. In the eastern states whenever there has been a great strike, it has been the custom to introduce black labour. This custom will give place to the intro- duction of "Honest John," whose numberless good qualties I cannot enumerate. A. R. Colquhoun has just issued a book "China in Transformation " an 1 so far as I am able to judge, it may be safely taken as a guide by those who will have to study this question. The writer starts out with the opinion that China is bound to play a most important part in the future history of all peoples, Western as well as Eastern. "The Chinaman," he says. "fulfils in the highest degree the ideal of an intelligent hu- man machine. His predominant quality, that which marks the Chinese as a race,whether at home' or abroad, is beyond doubt, his industry. Com- bined with the appetite for hard work the China- man has two highly important qualities—docility and temperance. There is no end to his patience He demands no comfort, still less luxury. He will ' work outrageously long hours. He has a robust muscularity, and to cap all has an intellectual capacity which may rank with the best in Western countries." It requires no great fore- sight to be able to foretell that, when the spirit of progress is really abroad in the land, when modern improvements and methods are studied and adopted i , by the people, the Chinaman will occupy a lending ' position among his contemporaries in the worli of I commerce and manufactures. We must not fancy the time a long way off when the Chinaman will share with us all our mental and mechanical appli- ances. Did the Western world really know how near this time is to us, it would stand not only astonished, but appalled. There are many English- men who have a great objection to the introduction of Western ideas into China. They know that the cheapest thing in China is a man. Having observed the progress made by the East Indians in manu- facturing, they are satisfied that their achievements will be thrown in the shade when the Chinese are taught the use of improved machinery. I see from the lengthy telegrams from England. published in American papers, that England has all the trade just now, that she requiree. This is, in a sense, satisfactory, but what shall we say of the future in face of the Trade Reports now daily appearing in the American press? I refer to the increased export trade of American goods to England. These Reports quote liberally from the British press, and we must regard with surprise the statements made with regard to the British and American shoe trade which appeared in the "Glasgow Herald" of January 14th. In an elaborate review of the trade of Scotland in 1898, which was published on that date,the Herald, among other things remarked: Eighteen hun- dred and ninety-eight opened gloomily in the boot and shoe trade. . . To add to the dulness among manufacturers, a very large portion of our colonial trade was fairly wrested from us by our Amelcan cousins, who, at the moment of writing, have prac- tically the whole boot and shoe trade of Western Australia and Africa. Not only so. but American manufacturers during the year puQhei oir home manufacturers severely for the boot and shoe trade of the United Kingdom, and have firmly established themselves in our midst. To our annoyance and irritation it must be candidly admitted that their manufactures for beauty of style, handsome appear- ance and perfection of fit excel ours. . . The question continually asked in the boot and shoe trade is: How comes it that America is able to de- liver to our very doors boots and shoes at prices considerably less than can be accepted by eur own manufacturers ?" American manufacturers under- selling the Britisher in his own markets and on his I own ground may seem somewhat of a puzzle. and is only partly explained by the Ameri- san Consul at Birmingham. Mr. Tfaistead quotes a manufacturer as saying " Busieess is business, and when your people *can sell cheaper they certainly should- and will make the sales; but I very much fear that, owing to their inexperience in foreign trade, they are going to de- moralize prices the world over. When big profits are in sight and possible, they seem ready to give away the benefits of your grand natural resources, of your manufacturing brain; and tremendous energy to Kaffirs,Cape Colonists and other Africans, to Australians. West Indians, South Americans, Japanese, and even to the "heathen Chinee," for a petty profit,simply because they have no know- ledge offoreign trade and certainli no trade pati- ence. They will lower all market values, Even in this country Americans are selling nearly every- thing for lower prices than are necessary." Mr. Halstead seems to have been impressed with this comment, and advises American manufacturers to 'charge all the traffic will bear. He quwes from a circular published at Wolverhampton, England, by the principal concern of that place dealing in bolts aud nuts,in which the statement is made that American makers are selling bolts and nuts in the English markets at from £2 to .C 4 per ton less than the prices ruling in that country. "The quality of the bolts and nuts," the circular says, "is fully equal to the very best quality made in England." Under the circumstAnces the Consul thinks it is hal judgment for the Americans to cut prices in this fashion. They ought, he thinks, to get as much as they can for their wares, which he says they can do by studying the market more closely. A similar cendition of things pertains in all lines of trade. Even the Midland Railway C3mpany has just placed a large order of some 20 locomotives , with an American firm. American writers seek to gather from all this a lesson, and point the moral as an object lesson to the American Trade Unionist, who, while he has the ruin brought about by strikes pointed out to him, is patted warmle on the back because he refrains from the objectionable practices , which have been specified by the Mater Builders Association in the ultimatum recently presented to the Plasterers Unions, throughout the United King- dom, and which I have before me. In another re- port it is stated that the power of the Trades Unions is gone so far as Great Britain is concerned. The British employers are forming a gigantic com- bination, to fight the workmen with their own weapons. The engineering feaeration, which I proved so powerful in the recent strike, has invited employers in all the trades to "crush the tyranny" of trades unionism. One object of the combination into secure legislation favourable to the employers. i The Railroad Review asserts that one firm has placed £35,000 at the disposal of the organizations Parliamentary Committee. It may seem to some of my readers that I have taken up more space than is desirable with these matters, to me it seems of the utmost importance that the workman should know, as well as his em- ployer. what is going on in the world. 1 look upon the recent skirmishing in China, and the war America has just had with Spain as the beginnings of such events in the labor world as history has no record of.

He illustrated his sub- jet by referring to some of the marvellous displays ot the wisdom of Cod in nature. The Rev. BAC., very effectively contributed an organ solo. The service was also taken part in by Mr. axles and Mr. George Wallington. CHRIST AND SOCIAL JUSTICE.

The Rev. F. E. Powell, M.A., delivered an address on Sunday afternoon in St. James's Church, on "Cerist and Social Justice." At the outset the rev, gentleman said : We appeal to Christ and we find that He claims the whale of life as his. He bids us ask for those things which are reqiiiii!e and necessary as well for the body as the soul. We appeal to the Bible, and we find that therein is the ideal of Gid which is slowly being realised. If we would make by prayer and effort for His goal and not try to estebish schemes of social regeneration of our own the Seal! Order would be more quickly reached. We appal to natural science, and we find there certain indications of social progress, certain lines of advance similar to the physical and biolegical progress which astronomy, geology, and biology reveal. The devious and rugged course of social proeress is due to the mys- terious presence of moral evil' in the world. Progress sometimes may have the appearance of retrogressioo, hut the ascent, though spiral, is ever upward and on- ward. As a concrete illustration embedying in one con- centrated focus the awful de ath-struegle of justice with injustice, the lecturer instanced the French Revolution. In it we had a powerful warning te those who desire a social revolution by violent, means. The very people who rose up against deereded and awful tyranny and oppression perpetrated the worst vices of tyranny them- selves. In the sacred names of liberty, equality, and fraternity the Robespierres and Marats co.nreitted the most shocking crimes. Since then we have learned that ordered evolution is better than violent revolution ; that s"cietyis an organic entity subject te the laws of growth and development. And so while the reformers of 1789 would have swept away the past into a silent oblivion, and tried to begin society entirely afresh, we hay - learned to find the best hope for the future in the past, and to build up what oueht to he on what has been and what is. In the Lord's Prayer, just as social order is expressed in the petition "Thy will be done as in heaven so in °era.," just as srcial progress finds expression in the petition " ihy kingdom come as in heaven so in earth," so social justice finds expression in the prayer, " Give us this day our daily bread." For in it we are taught not ta ask for the simplest thing our- selves without askingir, for o:hers as w-11. The erred we should eat is God's Bread. Bread which, by gambling or dishonesty, or thieving, or sweating, is filched from his neighbour is the devil's bread, ana not God's. No wealth is honest wealth which has been accumulated by taking advantage of the weakness or igncrance of our brether, and tor which reciprocal service has not been rendered. Wealth is only earned in accordance with social justice when the social order is served, when the common weal is furteered.

div.head: WORD TO WOMEN.
div.p: A WORD TO WOMEN.

Popular as Mother Seigel's Syrup is with both sexes for the various ills common -to them, it is the women who speak of it in terms of warmest praise—and ;with good reason. It seems especially adapted to the troubles which are distinc- tively and peculiarly theirs. At the critical period of life they de- rive from its use a degree of relief and benefit not obtained from any other medicine. The sense of pressure on the brain which makes the head feel as if it would burst, is quickly abated by a few doses of the Syrup. The melancholy and profound depression of spirits, which develops sometimes into acute mania, and not infrequently. ends in self-destruction, gives place to a wholesome and natural cheer- fulness under its influence. It dis- pels those conditions of the blood which cause the tendency to can- cer, tumour and other morbid growths. By carrying off the im- purities of the blood it prevents the formation ot varicose veins and other evils of a clogged) and cor- rupt circulation. It removes that sensation of bloating, warms and stimulates the stomach, and takes away the feeling of coldness and insensibility from the hands and feet caused by excess of blood in the head. It cures also the trembl- ing of the limbs. By thus equalising the flow of the blood Mother Seigel's Syrup does away with the hot flushes followed by chills, and creates a genial and even warmth and sense of comfort throughout the system. As a remedy for the habitual costiveness which is so common at this period, the Syrup excels all other preparations. It moves the bowels gently and keeps them free and natural. By so doing it also stops heart palpitation, nervous- ness, and weakness—in short, this most excellent medicine meets every requirement of the crucial epoch of woman's life as nothing else does.
