div.head: SAD SUICIDE OF A ViTIRRINGTON
div.p: SAD SUICIDE OF A ViTIRRINGTON
GENTLEMAN.

On Friday afternoon, about 3.20. Mr. Frank Con- life, of the firm of Tattersall Cunliffe, Holmsfield Tannery, Howley, Warrington, committed suicide under distressing citcumstances. It appears that Mr. H.erbert Crosby, his clerk, went into the Tannery Yard and on his return he heard moans proceeding from Mr. Cunliffe's private offi3e. On entering be fosnd Mr. (Jun Life lying on the floor in a pool of blood with a revolver near his right hand. On ex- amination it was found that a bullet had entered on the right side of the ear,had burst the skull, and gone through at the left side. Mr. CunMrs was in a dying condition and Dr. Adams was sent for but on his arrival life was extinct Deceased was conveyed to the mortuary at the Cemetery where his body lies pending an inquest. The revolver, it may be stated, was a six— chambered one, and there was another chamber undischarged. Mr. Cuuliffa was about 40 years of age and resided at Liverpool. S 3 far as can be as— certained, there was nothing on his mind to lead him to commit the rash act. INQUEST AND VERDICT.

Oa Slturday afternoon, Mr. S. Brighous7, county coroner, conducted an iiquiry in ths Parade Room of the Police Station, tcuching the death of Frank Cunliffe, managing director of the firm of Tattersall Cunliffe Limi.ed, tanners, Howley, who shot himoelf in his priv- ate office on Frilly afternoon.—Mr. R. Anderton was fonman of the jury. Walter Cunliffe, solicitor, Liwrpool,said deceased was his broth,r. He lodged in Liverpool, and wa3 manag- ing director of the firm Dceased was 40 years of age.He last saw him alive on Friday. He left him at the works at two o'clock in the aite.ruoon. In coase:juence of the sate of deceased's health he th)ught it necessary on Tuu-sday to take him to a doctor. They saw Dr. Glynne, of Liverpool, who said deceased's coldition was attribu- tab!e to overwork, and ads 'd him to go to a hydra.. pat hic institution and afterwards for a sea voyage. A Juror: What was his complaint ? Witness : The doctor did not name it. Deceased said that somPon, had been circulating a rumour against him in Warrington.

A Juror : Toe doctor should have said what his elm. pl lint was. Deceaied must have ben suffering from general debility. Witness said that drceved lived in Bewsoy-stre,et for a good mAny rats. Be was always of a very quiet dis- position. They had no idea that he intended to take away his life. Whni he received the doctor's advice he said he could not b c.*) to a hydro. The doctor told him to take a_week's holiday. _ _

By the C)roner : Be had ncver takln any lengthy holiday. Re pail very clo.r, attention to business. By Inspector He did not know deoeased kept a revolver in his office. There were two guns in cases there.

Herbert Crosby, clerk in the employ of the company, said decease:l came to business at the usual time on Fri- day, and was in his ofcejn the afternoon. Witness saw him at 3-23 sitting his chair. Nothing unasuat occurred th n. He (witness) went into the yard, and was there about two minutes. When he came back ne thought be tiv-,u2lit he heard a snore in dece4s7d's office. He took no notice, but then h 3 heard a groan: He saw a ware- houseman.Rnd told him he tlought there was something wrong. They went to the office, and found deceased lying on the floor in a NO of tlood. Wit-,ess telephoned for Dr. Adams, who, on arrival, pronourlced deceased to be dead. Witness sent a message to the police. He subsequently saw the revolver. He had never seen it before.
Inspector Phillips said it was a new Colt's revolver, conttining one di,charged cartridge, Toe other barrels were empty..
Witne;s said that whoa hi returned to the office after dinner (on o'clock) deceased asked aim t 3 go a walk for an hour.
The C 'toner: Had you noticad anything strange about him ?
Witness :
He had been very quiet.
It was elicited that decease-LI was a very steady man. Witness s lid he was smoking a cigarette two minutes be. fore he shot himself.

Ernest Clayton, in the employ of the Company, said the clerk told him on Fr:day afternoon that Mr. Canliffe was making a peculiar noise in his office. He (witness) did not think anything was wrong, and went back to his work. 'Th c:erk afzerwardi returned and said that Mr. Curiliffe was lying in a pool ot blood. Witness went into the office and unfastened deceased's tie and collar. He was lying on the floor. There was a wound in his head. The revolver was under his leg. Witness told Crosby to bring the flreman. Witncss had noticed that decease] was strange in his manner. He was very par- ticular about his work, and, in fact, was an ideal manager. He had Wen strange during the last fort- night. Witness could tell by (ha way he did certaia things that something was wrong. He had been very quiet, and that was unusual.
- A Juror: Had anything been troubling bim beside business ?

Witness : Nothing to my knowledge. The jury returned a verdict to the effect that deceased had c mmittml suicide during a fit ot temporary insanity, brought on by overwork, and .;passed a vote A condolence to the family and relatives.

CONSERVATIVE MEETING AT WINWICK. He said he nad much pleasure in proposing the election of Mr R S:one as chairman of the Win wick Polting District for the ensuing year.—Mr J W Knowies seconded, and Mr Holland Owen supported. The motion was unanimously carried. The Chairman proposed the re-election as vice-chairman of Mr. Owen. Mr. J Knowles seconded, and the motion was carried unanimously. Mr. Cooper was re-appointed lion secretary and trea- surer of the district. The Chairman proposed that Messrs. J Swinton and S Thomason he re-elected. delegates to the Council. Mr. W Massey seconded. and it was carried. The cowmittee were also re- elected. with power to add to their number. The Rev. W Williams moved tte following resolution: "That this meeting desires to express its unabated confidence in Her Majesty's CLivernmeut,and whilst assurirn, them of continued support in the future, sincerely hopes that teir efforts to promote the best interests of the B 'tiS! Jmpire may be brought to a most succesful issue." The resolution wa,s carried unanimouslv.

it vital ty concerns special parts. It is reasonable to contend that goods and passengers conveyed long distances without change should be charged at lower rates than others. We must admit that through bookings should have a preferential rate. But the rate may seriously injure local trade and agriculture, and then it is distinctly bad and ad- verse to the general interest. To adjust the two kinds of rates is not easy, but if the through rate plinciple be not too unfairly applied there will be little cause of complaint. It often occurs, however, that all local goods ara seriously handicapped by these preferential rates, and that harm is done to agri- cultural products and the local industries. In the new glare of publicity which has been cast upon irregularities of this nature we detect an indiffer- ence to local complaints which is lamentable. When this is the case single firms and persons can do little. They must act through Chambers of Commerce or of Agriculture, or local bodies of a more specific character. There is little hope of redress in any other way. We say boldly that if the agricultural organisations had been more sturdy in looking after railway rates they would have been less injured by foreign competition and better able to fight the battle of profitable pro- duction. Happily, several railway cotnpamies are alive to their duties in these matters, and we honour them for their zeal and foresight. Where- ever the contrary is the case the public should be up and doing.

TIE important deputation to Mr. Chaplin and Mr, Walter Long, on points affecting tuberculosis legislation, had much that was reasonable to urge in support of their demands. There are, of course, some obvious difficulties in the way of granting compensation for animals which are seized and con- fiscated for the benefit of the public health, but in principle the request is not unjust, and many arguments could be cited in its favour. The aboli- tion of private slaughter-houses and the substitu- tion of public abattoirs is a reform that has long been urged on humanitarian and sanitary grounds, and we are sorry that in this connection the Butchers' Association did not render effective support to a proposal which has been unwisely held to be harmful to the trade as a whole, and has certainly been opposed by the London section. The suggestion, that a uniform standard should be devised,to abolish an existing anomaly,whereby an animal seized and condemned in one district would be passed as sound in another, cannot in any way be objeated to. Theoretical differences of opinion as to the soundness or unsoundness of an animal must of course always exist, but that does not prevent the adoption of a uniform test or rule, by which the inspectors must b 3 guided. The existing anomaly is ridiculous and unfair, for it may assist one trade competitor at the expense of another.

The annual report of the fourth National Coun- cil of the Evangelical Free Churches presented at Liverpool is a most encouraging document. It is sad to remember that the first report was pre- sented at the Birmingham Congress, which met under the late Dr. Berry's presidency; but since that day five years ago a new organisation has come into existence, and it has more than justified itself by the immense advance that is recorded to- day. It is a matter for the deepest congratulation that, although the councils represent so many shades of theological thought and differences of political opinion, no serious fissures have shown themselves. There are six hundred councils,diverse in everything,perhaps, save a common and sincere love of free religion; and it is almost miraculous that no fissiparous tendencies should exist. It is gratifying, also,that federation should ba procee - mg sl) steadily abroad. Distinct developments are reported from South Africa, Canada, the United States, Australia, New Zealand, and Jamaica, where, as the result, a needed impetus has been given to evangelical work among the people. Since the federation movement first began a wave of spiritual revival has been observable among most of the Free Churches and though it has been quiet in its working, :it has been none the loss powerful. The Churches have been greatly strengthened, an the Roman Catholic assault upon them which Cardinal Vaughan fore- shadowed at the . Hanley Conference of the Catholic Trutle Society some years ago, has failed so completely that in all probaryility it will not I be renewed systematically or with hope of success.

div.p: MARCH 17th 1899.

THE common method of deal- Pension or ing with the financial side of the Relief. Old-Age Pension question is to represent it as an addition to existing Poor-law relief, and as therefore involving the expenditure of ever so many millions more a year. It is time We obtained clearer notions on the subject. Pen- for the thrifty only do, in a way, involve this double expenditure, but not to the extent which is generally calculated. Roughly speaking, it may be taken as arguable that one-half of the existing Poor-law relief expenditure would cease if pensions Were given at sixty-five. There would be fewer Persons in the workhonses and there would be fewer persons receiving outdoor relief.Further,the families now supplementing outdoor relief for the aged heads by their own expenditure and accom- 15:Iodation would be relievedof the strain,and there- fore in less danger of conaingeen the rates in turn. There would be a general improvement of all the families of which one member is now nearly always ln receipt of some form Of Poor-law assistance. There would also be an improvement in all work- ing-class families now on the edge of destitution, because the assistance they render to disabled members of the age of sixty-five would be supple- mented by the pension. In other words, we ought to regard the pensions as a form of poor relief, coming from the national exchequer instead of the rates, and as necessarily relieving the rates both directly and indirectly. This idea seems to us to give strength to the advocacy of the non- selected het of pensioners, as well as to the equity Of a national poor rate. Assuming that at sixty- five every man, or widow, or spinster were en- titled to receive five shillings a week on applica- tion, it is obvious that the poor relief would diminish to a very considerable extent, and that collections of elderly people in workhouses would be almost unnecessary. It may be cheaper to maintain them in this way, leaving out cost of buildings and establishment charges,but it would be better for the community at large that such per- sons should be living among their friends, as long as their behaviour is beyond reproach. That as, the old-age pension all round is relief, and if it came out of national taxation it would leave been contributed to by every taxpayer, and must not be regarded as if it were so much addition to, instead of a considerable redaction of, ordinary poor-rates. This simplifies the whole question, and- it is in this direction we must bend our thoughts. Pensions by merit are admissible on paper, but pensions for all, as relief, not as some- thing earned, would have several advantages. The wise, the industrious, and the thrifty would still prefer to provide for their own old age. The ill-behaved would get relief at a certain age, na- tional if they were fit for it, in workhouses if they 'were, unfit for a life in a decent family. The moral effect of the national pension, as distinct from poor relief, might not be very great. It woulletill be something. But it will be said that the cht.nce of a pension would discourage all the self-regarding virtues. We doubt it. The old man or woman able to dispense with assistance Would still head the list as the aristocrats of the :Poor. The others would follow in their order.

Is the Parliament of this country subservient to the Standard Oil Trust of America? This is a question to which people might reasonably expect an answer, as a result of the debate on Mr. H. J. Reckett's Bill for the raising of the petroleum oil flashpoint. Notwithstanding the weight of public opinion in favour of the flash-point being raised to 100 deg., and the able arguments of the sup- porters of the Bill, Parliament has decided against it. On what grounds it is difficult to say. There has been a suggestion that the Bill was conceived in the inteeests of Scottish and Russian oil pro- ducers, but we cannot imagine any sane and fair- minded legislator attaching weight to this insinua- tion. It is an undoubted fact that the Standard Oil Trust has been busy safeguarding itself, and its emissaries have been very active among the members of Parliament, but we are un- willing to think that there can have been any undue influence exerted. Yet it is a remarkable thing that a majority in the House of Cemmons should declare themselves against a Bill, the sole object of which is to ensure the safety of millions of the country's inhabitants. Mr. Jesse Collings said there were 10,000,050 lamps burning every night —and by the action of Parliament everyone of these ten million lamps is rendered liable to ex- plode with murderous effact. That is what the whole thing amounts to. Oil at a flash point of only 73 degrees is "murder-oil," and if its use is continued then we can only expect a continuance of frightful fatalities. The change to a flash-point of 100 degrees would not make any very material difference in price,and the theory that it wonld, advanced ostensibly in the interests of the workingman, we regard as entirely fallacious Then the suggestion that the adoption of a safety lamp would remedy the evil is only another way of begging the question. BURNING FATALITY AT RUNCORN.

Oa Tuesday, Mr. J. E. Worsley, coron-r, held an in quest, at the Runcorn Police Station, OR the body 0 the infant daughter of Thomas Jones, 6, Poole-lane, Run- corn, who died on Monday last fram toe eff ;es of burns received the previous day.—From the evidence submit- ted, it ppears that on Sunday morning, during the temporary absence of the mother, the little girl obtained possession of a box of matches, and it was supposed must have set fire to her clething through accidentally igniting them. Hearing the screams of the child Mrs. Jones rushed into the house, and her husband who was in bed, came downstairs, and both parents immediately extinguished the flames, not, however, before the lower extremities of the child had been severely burnt. The parents obtained 1-nseed oil from Mr. T. Pendlebury, the Royal Oak, and dressed the burns. Shortly afterwards Dr. Bankes, assistant to Dr. Robinson, was summoned, and everything possible was done to alleviate the little one's sufferings, but despite all care she passed away in great agony at about noon on Monday.—The jory who expresPd sympathy with the parents, returned a ver- dict of" Accidental death." We understand that the jury, police, coroner, an I Dr. Robinioa showed their heartfe't sympathy with the pow parents in a very ap- preciable degree,and presented them with the larger por- tion of their fees. This was done on the suggestion of Police Gonotable Gregory.

div.head: MERSEY- MISSION TO SEAMEN.
div.p: MERSEY- MISSION TO SEAMEN.

The annual report of the Mersey Mission to Seamen Society, it to hand, for the year, 1893, discloses some interesting facts proving the utility of the Society in a pro-eminent degree. The far-reaching influence of the Mission work may be seen when we state that an one centre alone, viz., Hanover-street Institute and Sailors Home, the atteadances of seamen at divine worship amount 3d to 10,715, whilst to those should be added the daily congregations attending the Mission Churches at Bootle, Runcorn, Garston, Birkenhead, and Ellesmere Port, as well as the daily services held on board H.M.S. " Eagle," the cadet .thip "Conway." and the training ship " Indefatigable." The report of Mr. W. Shaw, lay minister, Runcorn, of the work done in the Runcorn Branch is very interesting. The services at the Mission are described as hearty; the Sunday school work encouraging, and, we give an extract, "for cleanliness and behaviour the boat children will. I blieve, compare with any other children in the town." Toe report specially mentions that the Society's thanks are doe to Sir R. A. L. Brooke, Misses Hayes, Mn. Garrett, Mrs. C. ElazAteurst, Mrs. W. J. Crosiley, Messrs. J. Meadow- croft, J. K. Di 'gee (hon. secretary), W. Shaw (licensed reader). J. Stokes, R. Shaw (organist), and J. B. Arthur, and the mane kind friends who have assisted in furthering the work at Runcorn. During the year 190 bundles of literature were given to Seamen; 178 letters written by them ; 7 total abstainers were enrolle ; upwards of 250 woollen articles (priucipallylworked by the children of Frodsham) were distributed, and numerous entertainments, hot pot supoers, etc., were promoted for the benefit of the sailor. Many Rick sos- men had been vieited, and shelter was in numerous cases secured for disabled seamen of Foreign nationalities. On the whole the Runcorn Branch have accomplished sterling work.

div.head: RUNCORN CHARACTER SKETCHES.
div.p: RUNCORN CHARACTER SKETCHES.
No. 4. BY Q. E. F. D.

It has long been a moot question whether eccen- tricity is a quality indicative of genius. The argu- ments pro and con are many. Numerous examples gre to be found which will substantiate the differ- ent theories which are offered by the advocates of each. One thing, however, is pretty clearly veri- fied ; it is that eccentricity only attaches itself to those who have either a superabundance of earthly treasure, or are possessed of faculties which raise them out of the rut of the common. When a monied or talented man is possessed of a few idio- syncrasies he is termed an eccentric genius. When, however, a man in ordinary circumstances and of average intelligence possesses a few peculiarities he is known by a someone harsher name. Peabody, the American philanttiropis% was an eccentric genius; James Con, of Ship Canal fame, is termed slightly demented. Perhaps, after all, genius, ec- centricity, and madness are somewhat closely allied to each other. If, however, it be admitted that a genius has his quips and cranks and that these pe- culiarities are a sign of mental power, then there are residing in our midst geniuses of the first water.

The individual under notice presents a remark- able character. Not only is he eccentric, but he is undoubtedly possessed of strong mental faculties. It is not generally known that previous to his re- siding in the town he had a distinguished career as a student; taking a degree which testad all his powers and tried his perseverance to the utmost. He has now, consequently, become a recognised authority among his fellow craftsmen. The statement that he is one of the cleverest practitioners in Runcorn could be easily proved. It will by the careful reader have been previously noticed that he is an import into the town; and it will not be a matter 13r surprise when the fact is noted that he is of the GEelic race. We are aware of the wonderful combination of enterprise and caution exercised by " the canny Scot "; it is pro- verbial that the Scotchman always manages to forge ahead of his competitors. The remark that when the North Pole is discovered a member of this wonderful nation will be seen playing his ever- lasting bagpipe may prove eventually to be correct. Though somewhat far fetched the illustration only shows how the spirit of colonization seems to have gripped the entire nation, for the proud wearers of kilt and tartan are found occupying prominent positions all over the world,panetrating where others would never have ventured. It would, therefore, be strange indeed if Runcorn could not boast of possessing a real live Scotchman. And though our man cannot be said t 3 he addicted to the wearing of the Highland costume, he is so patriotic that the skirl of the pibroch or the sight of the tartan is sufficient to rouse all his latent clannish en- thusiasm.

To describe him is rather a difficult task. Heavy- looking, dark-bearded, a forbidding aspect, he does not look a man with whom a strong attachenent could be fornaed. Yet he is a singularly fine figure, notwithstanding the fact that he is somewhat past his prime. His massive brow denotes his strong intellectuality; his square jaw denotes his iron will; and hiss keen eyes at once proclaim the typical characteristic of the race—shrewdness. He is specially noticeable because of the student's stoop which tells of the weary hours spent over the book, burning the midnight oil, in earlier days. Perhaps his peculiar habit of continually gazing on the ground may have been contracted through thinking deeply over knotty problems, and his peculiar shuffling gait may be traced to the same cause. Who can tell? It is sufficient to say that he follows a profession which has benefitted the human race to an incalcul- able extent; has submitted happiness where pain I held all-powerful sway; has brought a smile to the I pallid countenance when hope seemed to have fled, and despair reigned supreme. No danger is too great to be faced, and even Death itself has been com- pelled to relinquish her grasp when her prey seemed to be secure. Our first mements'of existence are carefully watched by one of the fraternity ; our last moments also are soothed by the hand of one of the brethren. These facts are sufficient to show our in- debtedness to him. He holds in the town an impor- tant post, and being essentially strong-minded and outspoken, the inhabitants have been often ben.- fitted owing to his instrumentality. His official labours have been characterised by that carefulness simplicity and thoroughness which are seldom Ifound in combination, His productions are master- pieces of work and it would be difficult to find an- other person as well qualified to fill the official position which he holds. Though of an excitable disposition he is creditel with being a subtle reasoner. As a level headed matter-of-fact person it would not be an easy task to find his superior. His manner is bluff almost to rudeness; but though rough and rugged outwardly he is possessed of a warm heart. If he were to give he would cer- tainly never ask for it back. Perhaps he looks too much on the financial aspect of life, but then as we all labour for the" filthy lucre" it is not politic to cast any reflections on this ground. "Those who live in glass houses should never throw stones "is a proverb all should take to heart. A strong Churchman and also an ultra-Tory, he certainly does not display—paradoxical as the state- ment may appear—any inclination to Conservatism, but, on the other hand, holds the most advanced views on the majority of subjects which lie within his province. It would not be safe to assert that i he is an orthodox Churchman. Yet the man who. avowed that his conduct was not based upon the "Yea, yea; nay, nay "of the Gospel, would be one of those fearless ignoramuses who rush where " Angels fear to tread." As a faddist he may be termed a non,eariel ; and though by no means a good example of the genus bachelor iae is an unique specimen of a species of humanity which may be said fio be in many respects similar to the parent stock. It is not, therefore, a matter of wonderment when the fact is learned that he is an antiquarian; and is always in his element when ransacking musty archives and dabbling in . old relics which tell tales of an almost forgotten past. Space will not permit, nor is it desirable to enter into a category of his foibles. Those who re- cugnise the character can add the details to the skeleton outlines which have been but imperfectly traced.

There are five dis- tinct reefs in the property,several shafts have been sunk in the one hundred claims that the company possesses, and the tests in some cases were as high as 5 )z. to the ton. div.head: RUNCORN NOTES.
div.p: RUNCORN NOTES.
rBY. A CORRESPONDENTI

The dangeis of leaving matches within the reach of children has been sadly illustrated this week. in the lamentable death of the infant daughter of Mr. Thomas Jones, Poole-lane. The little three-year old could not have realised the danger that lurked in the apparently innocent match-box which brought about her sad end, indeed it is one of the most lamentable cases ever brought under notice. Parents should in all cases keep the match box in its proper place. The price paid by the bereaved parents is a very high one, but the hope is that the practice will not now be so lightly regarded, as it is in many homes, of " chucking ' the household match-box all over the place.

" BrunSwick "—the home of Runcorn Noncon- formity—has undergone a complete renovation, which now places the building in the front rank of any such in the district. The vestry-rooms, the gymnasium, cmild parlour, young mens' room, and last but not least the big kitchen have come in for a share of attention from "the mallet of the re- pairer, and the brash of the decorator." The large school-room presents a pleasant appearance,and the removatof the old gallery from three sides of it has considerably enhanced it. I heartily congratulate the friends who have worked so earnestly to secure the change. It is a monument to the esprit de corps of the Runcorn Wesleyans.

The Runcorn Wesleyan Cycling Club at its annual meeting on Monday, decided to join the N.C.U., which is indeed, a very wise step. The meeting was well attended and most of the old officers were re-elected. Mr. Bert Cooke (the popular captain) was vociferously re-elected, and the club did a good thing in refusing to allow him to withdraw. Mr. John Nancollis again acts as secretary, and Mr. George Payee as treasurer. The club is undoubtedly the most popular in Runcorn.

There will be but two elections for the position of Urban District Countillore, viz., in the Bridgewater Ward and in the Newtown Ward. In the first named ward where Mr. Shaw opposes Mr. W. Handley there are evidences of a stiff fight. Mr. Shaw re- presents the working classes, and is purely a work- ingman's candidate,and it is evident that the work- ingmen with whom he is very popular, will stand by him. Mr. Handley depends upon his past ser- vices to the town. So that the struggle between "New blood and old" is being keenly watched. From the evidences abroad it is very likely that "The staunch bloodhound will have to give way to the stauncher whelp."

A general surprise came in the retirement of Messrs. A.R. Norman and Jonathan florsefield. Why they took this course matters not, Bet certainly Mr. Norman has given up a safe se.at, as his popularity in the ward would have assured him success. The fight now lies between Dr. McKenzie and Mr. Samuel Walton and it appears but an insignificant one compared with the Bridgewater contest.

div.head: FOOTBA.LL.
div.p: FOOTBA.LL.

Runcorn meet Runcorn Recs. in the first round proper of the Northern Union Cup Competition, and this should assure their passage into the second round. The second round which comes off the following Saturday at Leigh is being freely com- mented upon, and it is generally thought that Run- corn will win. I hope so, but Leigh have tasted blood once, and will now prove twice as hard to defeat. Runcorn should not hold them too lightly.

LOCAL GOVERNMENT BOARD INQUIRY AT FRODSHAM. The Local Government Board forwarded notices of the inquiry to be held with respect to the borrowing of £3,400 for works of Water supply for Frodsham Lord- ship. The inquiry would be held by Mr. E A Saodford Fawcett,A.M.l.C.E., at the Boys' school Overton, on the 22nd of March, at 10.30 a.m. THE ESTIMATE FOR THE HALF YEAR. -

Mr. T. Wright submitted the estimates for the half year ending Lady Day 1899. The total capital for the current half year amounted to £6,223, and the nett pro- bable expenditure was esimated at £3,650 which showed a balance at Lady Day of £2,573. The probable expenditure during the ensuing half year ending Mic- htelraas was as follows :—Ganeral expenses (public health) £7OO, or less grant under Agricultural Rees Act £637; highways expenses £3,059, or less grant of £378 under Agricultural Rates Act, £2,841; repayment of principal and interest (highway loan) £l6O ; balance and contingency fund £2,505; making a total of £6,143. After deducting the probable balance lin favour of parishes at Lady Day 1899 the amount re- quired by contribution orders fram the overseers ie £3570. On an assessable value of £151,693 a rate of sid lin the £ would produce a sum of £3,478. and it was recommended that a call be made fer £3,570. The estimate was unanimously agreed to on the mo- tion of Mr. T. Wright, seconded by Mr. C. E. Linaker.
TITELWALL STREAM. -A DECISION COME TO.

Mr. Pilling reported that the whole of the members appointed en the committee t inspect and report on the stream met there on Thursday the aed March at 230 p.m. They were unanimous in recommending that the stream be thoroughly cleaned out, and then reduced in width to three feet, about the averaes width of the stream below the road culvert. When that was done the committee were of opinion that the stream wyald practic illy keep itself clean. The recommendation was adopted. TEL WALL BROOK names%

Plans were submited of buildings contemplated in the vicinity of an old road at Weston Point, by a Mr. Hewitt. Upon the plans was a note to the effct that a certain portion of land coloured blue would be given frea of cost to the local authority on condition that all drain- age was done in the high road, which the property abutted on, by the C uncil.—Considerable discussion followed, but it was generally expressed that the con- ditions were impossible.—The Clerk stated that the bye- laws of the Council required a 36 feet wide road in all cases.—Mr. Diggle considrred that it was p-rhans a , hardship for the whole of the 36 feet to come off the same side, and suggested that Mr. Hewitt be allowed to build within 18 feet of the centre of the road, and arm- one building on the opposite side would have to do Die- wise.—Eventually the matter was on the motion of Mr. C. E. Linaker, seconded by Mr. Talbott* referred to the Parliamentary Committee, with the object of consider- ing a general course with regard to tne width of the roads.

div.head: STRANGE FATALITY AT RUNCORN.
div.p: STRANGE FATALITY AT RUNCORN.

DEATH OF A WOMAN WHILST SHAKING A MAT. Mr. J. E. Warsley, coroner, held an inquest on Mon. day morning, at the London and North-WeEtern Hotel, Lowlands-L.-al, Runcorn, on the body of Mary Dun-. havin, aged 51, housekeeper to Mr. W•lliam Dunhavin, 53, Percival-lane, Runcorn,who died suddenly on Satur. oay morning last. _

Mr. Willia7na Dunb win, said he was an ass's:ant fore* man and reside] at 53, Percival-lane, Raocorn. The deceased was his housekeeper and had loam with him about eighteen Months. He saw her alive about 8.30 on the 11th inst, when she was in her usual good health. She had never complained of any pains in her side, but some time ago she complained of being troubled with wind. She bad not been medically attended within the last 4 months, but previous to that he thought she hart been attended by Dr. McDougall. If deceased hurried upstairs or did anything in a hurry it upset her. He believed she was about to shake a mat against a wall when she met her death. It was a heavy mat, and one that the deceased had shaksn in that manner many times before without complaining to him about it. Witness did not think it was anything unusual. He could not answer whether she had had a good breakfast or not, but usually she ate a very poor one, generally hay. ing nothlrg but a cup of tea and something light. De. ceased was about 51 years of are.

Agnes Washington, wife of Mr. John Washington, re- siding nest door to the previous witnese stated she saw the deceased on the morning of the 11th instant, at about 9.30. She went across the road to shake a mat acrainst the wall. Witness saw her fall down and went to her. Seeing there was sornethieg wrong she got assie- tance and aided by another neighbour carried deceased into the house and laid her on the sofa. Then she seat for Dr. McLennan. Mrs. Danbavin was deal before the doctor came, though it would only be about ten minutes from the first seizure before the doctor was on the spot. Deceased fell backwards with her hands on the mat and her legs appeared to double under her. They carried her in and after being laid on the safe, the deceased sighed twice and was gone. It Was not a very light mat. Deceased was a very quiet, nice woman. Witness bad not heard her complain, though she had known her for about 14 months.

Dr. Andrew McLennan, stated he was called in to see the deceased after death. HO had never previously attended her, and did not knew her. He attributed death to sudden failure of the heart's action aud front his external examination, and the evidence he had just listened to, considered Viere was nothing to suggest or indicate anything auspicious. _
The Coroner having summed up. the Jury returned a verdict of "Death from natural causes."

div.head: RE-OPENING OF 71:EIE BRUNSWICK
div.p: RE-OPENING OF 71:EIE BRUNSWICK
SCHOOLS.

ANOTHER LINK WITH THE PAST SEVERED. The Brunswick Schools, the memory of which is dear to the heat of all Wesle7ans, was on Taescla evening re-opened after undergiing a complete renova!ion though the chln,ze effected has unchubteny robbed the building—whioh has cradled the life and vitality of Rnn- corn Methodism for many a yer —of math of the dig-, tinetivenm it possessed, none can Bay the transforma- tion effected is not for the better.

The particulars of renovations have been 92 often and so ably commented upon, that to give them in this case in mere detail is unnecessary,whilst a general description will better serve the purpose. Eeeryone who en- tered the good old building was struck with the quaint gallery that encircled it, killing an impre;sive if some- what heavy appearance to the edifice. The principal alteration has been effected in the removal of the greater portion of that prominent feat ,re with the result that the building now presents a greatly enhanced appear- ance. The only part of the balcony that remains is that nearest the entrance, the removal of which would have entailed the complete remodeling of the porch and entrance, as well as the removal of the two staircases. Opposite the clock there is now a very fine rostrum, which, by the way, has been entirely made by the work- ingmen friends of the cause during their spare time; and we may also state that the whole of the labour ire zonnection with the alterations !vs been effected through the same generous agency. Of course, the joiner and decorator have also been at work, and the result of their joint labours impresses the beholder.

Mr. Timothy Simister prealded over the re-opening', happily celebrated in the form of a eonversazione, when the room was crowded. In his oppaing remark he highly complimented all upon the chanv effected, it was one that had blen neeld for some considerable

time. The Rev. C. W. L. Christien also spoke, and a high tribute was paid to the friends who had so gener- ously assisted in such a glorious consummation. The programme submitted included items by the Runcorn Orchestral Society, both overture and selection being tasteful, urisp, and well executed. The quartette party (Misses Birkett and Jones, and Messrs. R. Morris and John Birkett) pleased,. Mr. E. Kniv.ton was applauded for his contribution, as was Miss Taylor. The mandoline solos by Miss F Warburton were sympathetically re- ceived, and created a good impression. Miss Simkin's son.% was good. Mr. F. Littler recited in his usual man- ner, and a well-executed pianoforte solo by Miss Chrietien followed. The No. 2 Company of the Boys' Brigade, submitted an efficient drill, whilst the gymnas- tic performances of Messrs Hosker and Ii Dodd received great attention. The accompanist was Mr. George Bow- yer. The large audienee were highly pleased at the whole affair. No doubt some credit for the success of the gathering was due to th c tpital refreshments pro- vided by Mr. and Mrs. Nancollis, and which were so pleasantly served. The whole passed off without the slightest hitch, and the evening should mark another epoch in the history of Runcorn Methodism. The joinery work was carried out by Mr. Green, Top Locks, and the painting by - Mr. Garner, Halton-road, and the dispatch with which the work has been accom- plished speaks well for the repleteness of their respec- tive establishments.

div.head: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES.
AN EX-CONVICT THREATENS THE POLICE.

On Tuesday morning, at the Warrington Borough Police Court, before Mr. Garnet (in the chair) and Messrs. Birchall and Shaw Green, Michael Conner, last from Oldham, was charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Bank-street at 4.15 on Monday afternoon. Be pleaded guilty.—fle was also charged with having used threats towards P.C.'s Sankey and Marsh, and pleaded not guilty.—P.C. Sankey said prisoner was drunk in Bank street and used obscene language. He refused to go away when witness requested him, and he pulled his coat and vest off, and challenged • witness to fight. The latter obtained the assistance of P.C. Kane and took prisoner into custody. He threatened witness that whm he came out of gaol he would shoot bine.— P.C. Kane gave corroborative evidence.—P.C. Marsh Said that when prisoner got to the Police Station he struck out right and left at witness, and said he would do twelve months for him when he came out. He acted like a madman, and it took several officers to put him in the cells.—Prisoner said the officers knocked him anout scandalously and then rifled his packets. He had not been in Warrington for ten years.—Stiperintendent Monaghan said prisoner had been before the Court 42 times' which includ.d 12 times for assaulting the police. Be had had tea years' penal servitude for attempting to murder a police officer at Market-gate.—The mag.strates said the case was a bad one, but they would deal leni- ently with the prisoner. He would have to go to prison for one month with bard labour. RUNCORN BOATMEN FINED FOR CRUELTY TO A PONY. On Wednesday at the Warrington County Potty Ses- sions, before Mr. John Crosfield (in the chair)land Mr. John White, Charles Price, employed by Messrs. Richard Abel, canal boat carriers, of Runcorn, was summoned for working a pony whilst in an unfit state at Warring- ton, on March 7th, and Richard Price, the stable mana- ger Was summoned for allowing the same to be worked. DevUn said that at 2.30 on March 7th he saw Charles Price in charge of two ponies on the canal bank at Sankey Bridges. The animals were pulling a 70-ton load of sand. Witness noticed the grey pony was nothing but skin and bone, and he examined it. Several bruises were on the body, and over the left eye, on the near fore fetlock, and on the hind quarters were sores. They were recent wounds, and matter was oozing from them. The pony trembled" like a lesf " and eeemed to be starved. Witness called the attention of the driver to it. The latter said he did not think the a pony was as bad as it was, and he would take it home. Its legs were swollen.—Mr. Frank Kerfoot said the horse wag unfit to work. It was shivering from sheer exhaus- tion.—lnapector Canning, R.S.P.C.A., said the pony was in a shocking condition when he examined it on March eth. He had to help it out of the stable. It was simply a skeleton. He had never seen a pony in worse condi- tion.—The Chairmen said the way in which horses wore treated on canal banks was abominable. Richard Price would be fined £1 and costs, and Charles Price 51 and Costs.

ATTENDANCE CASES.—The following cases were proved by Mr. Jones, school attendance officer, and fines in- flicted :—Thomas Potter, labourer, 53 Watkin-street. 2s 6d ; Jam's Tatlock, labourer, Taylor's-yard, Winwlck-street,23 6d; ienry Chilton, baker, 2 Lee's-yard, Haydock-street, Sc ; Thomas Barton, labourer. 17 Chester-road, is ; James Early, 13, Stephen-street. is; William Hayes, labourer, 17 Dale-st.. 3s ; James Scully, 1, Rylands-court, 2s; Charles Camptell. labourer, 45 Old-road, 2s ; George Forster, labourer. 27, Napier-street, 23 6d. A. MARRIAGE ARRANGED.—An adjourned OM Was brought up when Mr. Taylor, police court missionary, reported that there was a satisf ',story improvement in the home of an unmarried couple (Edward James Barker and Winifred Noon) who were charged with neglecting their children. Mr. Birchall endorsed Mr. Taylor's remarks. The parties consented to be married, and a gold wedding ring had been bought with money from the poor box. it was stated that Canon Willisihad promised to marry them free of fees. WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. Geddes (chairman), and Mr. Birchall. COMMITTED TO THE "HOUSE OF CORRECTION."—Patrick Moran, Percival's Foil, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Horsemarket-street, at a quarter past elaven on Tuesday night, and with committing wilful damage amounting to 103 to a gas lamp att ,ohe 1 to the shop of Mr. John Finlayson, Horsernarket-street.—P.C. Stew ird said the defendant as soon as witness went up to him, jumped up and struck the lamp with his fist, smashing it.—Defeadant said he did it because he was drank. —The bench fined defendant 5s and costs for the first offence,and sent him to the " House f correction "for one month for the wilful damage.
waRKINGTON COUNTY PENT SESiIONS.
WEDNESDLY.—Before Mr. John Croefield (in the °IWO and

Mr. John White. A QUESTIoN OF RIGHT OF WAY.—James Nowd. farm labourer, employed by Mr. Warburton, was summoned for damaging a fence to the amount of 2s 6d on Lord Lilford's estate at Burtonwood on February 26th.—Mr. B. A. White prosecuted. and stated that defendant on the date in question was going through Bewsey Park to Burtonwood. When he got to the end of the drive he had to cross two fields to get on to the high road, There was no footpath through the fields. and defendant pulled the wire and thorns off a gate and aroma the fields to the annoyance of the farmers. The damage amounted to 2s 6d.—Ernest Hatton gave evidence bearing out this statement.and stated that when he spoke to defendant in the field he used bad language to him and lifted his hands several times to strike him He saU he would cross there again that night.—Defendant said he had passed through the fields continually far the past eight years and had never been stopped before.—The magistrates fined defendant 2s 6d for the damage and ordered him to pay the costs. MISCSLLINEOUS CASES.—Thomas Howard was summosled for having been drunk in charge of a horse and trap at Sankey on March sth.—P.C. Coupe said defendant, who was drunk, drove furiously along the highway aud collided with a fence. He was taken home by some friends. Fined 5s and costs.— Thomas Jones and James Tyler. of Sankey Bridges, were fined 2s 6d each for having been drunk and disorderly at Sankey Midges, on February 26th.—James Bellfield was fined 2s 6d for driving a cart without a light at Burtonwood I on the night of February 26th,—Richard Thompson Lowe,, Riaton Hall, who did not appear. was fined 5s and costs for driving a carriage without a light at Rixton, on February 25th.—James White. gro3er, VVinwick-street, was fined 5s for allowing his dog to be at large unmuzzled. on March 7th.

MONDAY..—Before Major C. W. Hazelhurst (chairman), and Messrs. James Mendley and A. R. Norman. Tam DANGERS -OF VAOCINATIoN —Walter Lawrence 49, Suffolk-street applied for a certificate of exemption, in respect of his child born on the 13th of November last. His objection was a conscientious one. He had lost one of his children through vaccination, and another had suffered from Its effects —The application was granted. DOG AT LARGE ~-7-(31-eorge Finney was summoned for allow- ing his dog to be at large on the 28th of last month. Defendant was represented by his wife, who pleaded guilty. —The Bench fined the defendant ss, and said a licence would have to be taken out if the dog was going to be kept. SCHOOL CASES.—The following persons were fined 6d and 4s 6d eosts in each case, for negleatine to send their children to school, on the evidence of School Attendance Offieers Bowyer and Howard :—John Harding (two cases), Shaw- street ; William Basnett, Gilbert-street ; William Harte, Cooper-street Joseph Jolley, Norton-street, ; Mary Thomp- son, Norton-street; George 0 olciough. Norton-street ; William Hayes, Spring Gardens; Joseph Wilson Mill Brow; Bernard Flannigan, Cooper-street; John Wakefield, Alcock street ; William Ashton (two cases), Waterloo-street. THE BENEFIT OE THE Dotenr.—William Yates, described as a pedlar, of Boole, was charged in custody with begging in High-street. Runcorn, on the 11th inst.. and also with being drunk and disorderly at the same time and place.—Prisoner pleaded not guilty.—Polize Constable John Upton stated thatlabout 4 p.m. on the 11th bast he received numerous com- plaints of the prisoner begging from young men and of his using bad lenguege to them if he re Tived nothing. His mode of procedure seemed to be that he begged list and if he re- ceived nothing he offered some laces for sale; if, however he was unsuccessful in selling any ha became abusive. Prisoner was also drunk at the%itne.—Prisoner at this point admitted he might have been drunk, but he never begged in,his life.— Henry Finney, professional swimmer, gave evidence of the prisoner begging from him, and corroborated the officer.— Prisoner said he never remembered seeing the last witness. He had only been in the town about five minutes when he was arrested. He had come in company with his wife that morning across the bridge from Widnes. He was a native of Bootle and never begged in his life .—Pee. Upton added that the prisoner had a pedlar's certificate.—The Chairman Geld they had decided to dismiss the charge of begging, for if prtsoner was convicted for that he would ease his certificate, and they were not desimus to' taking his livlittood from him. He would be fined be and 7s 6d coats on the other charge.— Prisoner thanked the Bench. A Morrie AND A PROMISE or MonE.—Blizabeth Barker was charged in custody, with being drunk and disorderly in Pool-lane, on Sunday lest.—Defendant pleaded guilty, and the case was proved by Police-Sergeant W Brewster who said he heard a row in Pool-lane and on going there found the prisoner very drunk, creating a disturbance, and also using abusive language.—The Bench committ-d - her to Knutsford for a month, and the Chairman remarked that if she again appeared before them they would deal with her unOer the new regulations when she would be liable to be sent for a much longer period. •• CARTING A • DRUNK' TO THE STA.TroN."—Patrick Fenney. Sutton, farm labouter, was so drunk on Sunday, the 12th March, that Police Constable Juette found it neces- sary to press in the services of a cart to bring him to the Runcorn Poli,e Station, where he was formally charged with the offence and lodged in the cells for the night. Juette further stated he found the man helplessly drunk and unable to stand under the window of the Red Lion, at Haltom—The Bench remanded the prisoner for a week on the application ef Superintendent Pearson.—Prisoner was bound over in his own reeognizances to appear next Monday morning.

div.head: RHODESIAN GOLD TRUST.
div.p: RHODESIAN GOLD TRUST.

The event of the past few days has bmn the interest taken in everything Rhodesian. Some ef the biggest financiers including the,Me;srs. Rothschild and the lead- ing Barlin bankers are 'now largely interested in Rho- desian gold propPrties. It is said that Mr. Cecil Rhodes has gone to Berlin to personally confirm the statements made about the groat mineral wealth of Matabeleland and ether portsof Rhodesia. The Rhodesian Gold Trust Limited, whose capital is 21.000,000 in shares of £1 each, has taken over In immense tract of GrAd-bearing reefs. They own 2.157 claims in the best known and most important parts of Matabelelo.nd and Rhodesia. According to the reports frtan their engineers on the spot, there are valuable old workings on many of these claims. Some of the properties are now being ctweloped, which means the flotation of a number of subsidiary companies with large profits to the parent company. me prosperity and success of the Rhodesian Gold Trust are now so well assured that ittis right we should draw attention to the low price, Bs. per share, at which its £1 shares are now dealt in on the London Stook Ex- change.

div.head: NORTHERN UNION. LANCASHIRE SENIOR COMPETITION.
div.p: THE NORTHERN UNION. LANCASHIRE SENIOR COMPETITION.

WIDNES THRASH WARRINGTON. Widnes were visitors to Warrington on Saturday, and were welcomed by one of the largest crowds of the season, fully 8,000 spectators being present. A large number came trona Widnes, who are commanding a lot of support this seasen by their many excellent perform- ances. Their successive victories over Oldham and Broughton Rangers put Widnes in the running for the championship again, and they took care to throw noth- ing away at Warrington. The hornesters had a very weak team, among the absentees being Bate, Ash.urst, Fish, Boardman, and Scholtze. Widnes had their strongest combination, Heslep being the only ab- sentee, and his place was well filled by Leyshon. Beautiful weather favoured the fixture, and the match was a most interesting one to watch. The referee was Mr. S. Williamr, Salford, and it cannot be said that he showed himself a capable interpreter of Northern Union Rules on Saturday. The teams were as follows : Widnes: Batey, full back ;J Hughes, Rispan, Nev;tt, and Martin, three-quarters ; Murphy and Dangles, half- backs ; Hammen, Handley, Aspey, Donnelly, Travis, Hamlin, E Hughes, and Levshoa forwards. Warrington : Hallam, full back ; Ratcliffe, Isher- wood. Wood, and Harris, threequarters ; J Wilcox and R Bate. half backs ; Taylor, Naylor, Morrison, Sullow, Swiit, Mason, Fairhurst, and Williams, forwards. There was a strong breeze blowing down the ground, and Isherwood was tortunat3 enough to win the toss. Warrington thus had the wind and sun, behind thnn in the first half. Aspey started the game for Widnes, and a quick dribble by the home forwards carried play to the visitors' quarter flag. Harris and Sallow put in useful punts, which further improved the position of the home team. Aspey marking safely. Bate gave Isherwood a quick pass, and the latter pun:e I down the field, and following up grandly tackled Batey near the line. Warrington now pressed herd, off-side play by Widneezoing unpunished. Harris put in a flying kick to the corner, Baty having to punt out of the field to save his charge. Fairhurst dropped fruitlessly, and Aspey again marked cleverly. Fr a time Warrington kicked shockingly and made no headway, but afterwards they played on Batey and found the County back very much at fault. A brilliant passing rub by Warrington carried play right to the Widnes line, Harris kicking across and Batey being held. Then Martin came away with an individual effort to centre where he was grassed by Hallam, who pu-, in a rousing punt which gave Warrington the upper hand again .B.s.tey let his side down by bad fielding, and some desperately hard scrimmaging near the cerner followed. Douglas had a kick charged down and Taylor rushed over amid great cheering. Hallam made a good attempt at goal. A moment later Fairhurst charged another kick and had the line at his mercy, but lack of speed prevented him' reaching the ball before it went in toecn at the corner. Isherwood tried a left-foot drop which was very near indeed, and for some time Warrington had much the best of the play. Widnes got into the home half by good passing. Alec Martin making a speedy run. Off side play by Widnes again passed mibter, and while play was in the home half Neyitt took a pass and dropped a neat goal. Warrington retaliated by rushing the game to the opposite end where Hughes was roughly handled by. Morrison and Naylor, the former of whom hurt him,snf. Smart play in the centre by Harris and Taber wood'again placed Widnes in diffi- culties, and Bsta9 was luelty to keep his line intact. End to end play followed in great excitement, which was trebled when Murphy ehereed Isherwood's kick down and had a clear run in, but went the wrong way and fell a victim to H allam. Widnes were an'', unrewarded however, for the same player made amends be dropping a second goal and giving his sile the lead. Widnes played up well, and Hughes was only just robbed of a try near the posts. The interval came with Widnes leading by 4 points to 3.

Everything favoured:the visitors on resumption, and they quickly asserted their superiority. Hallam was hard pressed but checked the attacking party by a clever mark. Harris made some headway from a pass by Wilcox, but Batey checked his progress at centre, Wood was slow and failed to check a smart movement between Rispan, Nevitt, and J. Hughes, the latter of whom passed all but the Warrington custodian who was safe. A long Beige of the Warrington line followed, and only vigoreus tackling kept Widnes out. Rispan got over at the corner but hoc pess-esion, and his try was not allowed. Marks by Fairhurst and Taylor staved off the danger temporarily, and a for- ward rush finally carried play to the Widnes half. Batey sent them back and another cross-kick by J. Hughes gave Martin a chance which he utilised finely and registered Widnes's first try in good position. Batey landed a goal. Martin made another effort later but was grassed in the corner. Loose play followed, and some bad passing by Widnes ended in Nevitt scoop- ing the ball up and running in behind the posts, Batey again improving. Hardly had the game got going be- fore the referee took it into his head t) enforce the play- ing the ball rule and Hallam was penalised, with the in- evitable result that Batey put another goal to the total. Warrington were entirely demoralised and gave a feeble display. Just before the close, Batey dropped at goal from his own half, the ball travelling just outside the posts and hitting the fence beyond. It was a magni- ficent—effort. Time arrived with the score reading: Widnes 5 goals, 3 tries (16 points) ; Warrington one try (3 points). BROUGHTON RANGERS v. WIDNES. The clese struggle between these clubs and Oldham for the championship of the section invested the match at Wheater's Field, Lower Broughtoc, on Wednesday, with the greatest interest. The positien before the metal was that Oldham had completed their series of the matches for 40 points. the Rangers with two matches in hand, ' had gained 38 points, and Widnes, with three matches to play, were 36 points. The Rangers, there- fore, by winning their remaining matches could secure the championship, whilst Widnes, if successful in their other matches, could tie with the other two clubs. Unfortunately neither team was at its full strength, Widnes suffering a serious loss in the inability of Murphy, their principal half back, to ploy through an injury, and the absence of Healop and Donnelly forward ; wnilst Steel, Whitehead, Mumbsron, Lazenby, and T. Black- lock did not turn out for the Rangers. The afternoon was fine, and a very large number of spectators— estimated at upwards of 15,000—were present when the match commenced. The teams were as follow : Broughtea Rangers : R Duck, full back; T Jackson, H C Chapman, A Barrett, and A Dan'son, three-quarter backs ; D damee and S James, half backs; J Blacklock, G Stickney,Lamb, C Thompson S Deakin, W Robinson, Brown, and Cleminson, forwards. Widnes: R J Batey, full back ; A Martin, T Nevitt, T Riapen, and J Huehes, three-quarter backs; E Douglas and W O'Brien, half backs; E Hampton, J Aspay, W Travis, R Thomas, T Handley, Hamlin, E Hughes. and Levant*, forwards. Aspey kicked off for Wide4s, and it soon !reams evi- dent that the players were in earnest. The visitors were especially smart, and before five minutes had elapsed the ball was rushed to the Rangers' quarter, where Nevitt got possession in the loose, and passed to J. Huekies, who ran in a betutiful try. This was a good beginning for the visitors, but the Rangers played up, and two minor points fell to them—me from a drop at goal by Chapman and the other the result of good play by Denson, that forced Widnes to tench down. Continu- ing to hold their own, Barrett slide a good mark near the centre of the ground, and Chapman placed a goal for the Rangers. Widnes then had the boss of the play, and after getting a minor point Batey placed a penalty goal. At half time Widnes led by one goal and a try to a goal. The visitors commenced the second half by forcing a minor point, but they failed to retain their lead, the Rangers in the latter part of the game having much the best of matters. A good punt in by D. James sent the ball in front of the Widnes posts. Chapman failed at goal, but five minutes later Chapman took a long drop at goal, and, following', up smartly,he regained possession and secured a try, which he also placed into a goal. The Rangers afterwerle had the game their own was', and passing between David James, Chapman and Jackson ended in Jackson adding an unconverted try,while Chapman dropped a goal a little later from the field of play. Final score :—Rangers, three goals and three tries (15 points) ; Widnes, one goal and one try (fie points). Chapman stoed out very conspicuously in the match and had a large share in gaining the victory for his side.

div.p: RUNCORN GAIN POINTS AT STOCKPORT.

Runcorn is withont doubt the most popular team that appears at Stockport, and there was naturally a good attendance at the E lge:ey Park enclosure on Saturday to witness the return fixture. Worsley re-appertred in the borne team afcer an absence of eight weeks, whilst Runcorn were without Jolley and Warder. Farmer started operations against a strong sun, Simister reply- ing to midfield. Houghton then got possession, but was too well tackles to get far. Followieg a bad pass by Booth there was some loose play which resulted in Run- corn getting into the home territory, and then Faulkner punted over the bar. Alter a mark by Grange C. Butterworth got hold,and, after a good run, was tackled by Sands, but still he managed to transfer to his brother. Saville made an effort to get through,but to no purpose. Runcorn were kept busy defending their line, and relief came by a kek from touch. Orem here put in some good play, then Farmer took the ball, but in pass- ing it caught the referee. Runcorn were penalised, Saville makiag a good but futile shut for goal from half- way. Wilkinson and C. Butterworth then tried to move, but were checked. Sands fumbling the ball Runcorn were soon at the home line, and Stockport saved by 'tic zing dead After some play at centre Burrows kicked up field, and Heuehton had to save. Play again came to centre. where Stockport, with the sun at their backs, had, if anything, a slight pull. Saville had another chance of shining trom a penalty kick,but again ' missed, and when the teams crossed over the scoring board was blank. Garside restarted, and Both passed to Rebinsan, but he was colarei before he could make any headway. Then Jones g3t possession from a scrum- mage, and made for the home line, and although he managed to clear Saville, Worslery overtook him just in time to prevent what appeared to be a certain score. Stockport bad a spell of attacking, RohinPon being very prominent. Relief came by a long kick up the field, after which J. .Butterworth tried to drop a goal, but failed. C. Butterworth made a mark, from which Houghton steerA a goal in good style. Runcorn were pegging away in the home 25, and Robinson just man- aged to check J Butterworth in time. Houghton tried to drop, but without ruccess. After a mark by Worsley, C. Butterworth got over at the corner, no goal coming from Houghton's kick. Just before time Saville ran to meet the ball, but failed to gather, and Walker following up added another three points. J. Butterworth this time took the goal iliac, without success, so that the home team once more suffered defeat by one goal and two tries (eight points) to nothing. ROCHDALE HORNETS v. ST. HELENS.

At Ro?,hdale, before 4,000 spectators. Good kicking by Field and Every gave the Hornets the advantage,and Rigg made a fruitless drop at goal. Foulkes relieved to the centre, where Kruger lost ground with a had pass. Wight man punted out of touch, and Boyle's reply was charged down by Harrison. who gathered the ball, and scored a fine try. Rigg failing at goal. A penalty to Doherty enabled the visitors to press, and a dead ball was forced. Capital play by Rigg was shown, after which Field got away, and passed to House, who was dispossessed by Foulkes. Every made a good run from half-way, being pulled down two yards short of the line and Davies almost scored from a pass by Jardine. The Hornets pressed until Every dropped at goal, Hardiker following up and gaining a try. Field also added a try, Rigg placing two goals. Half time score :—Rochdale Hornets, two goals and three tries ; St. Helens, nothing. Barnes restarted, Carney handicapping his side by get- ting off-side. Field passed to House, who kickei over the line, but Foulkes kicked the ball dead. Simpson headed a dribble which was distinctly dangerous, but Every pluckily ran the ball out. Taylor was ordered off for foul play at tbis point, and St. Helens were sub- sequently one man short. Liversedge was prominent with spiritel running, Wilson and Rigg bringing him down in tura. DAVieR also ran and passed to /louse, whom Barnes brought down spendidly. St. Helens pressed after this,hut play fluctuated considerably. Every and Kruger were very tricky, and Kruger added a try before the finish. Result :—Rochdale Hornets,two goals and four tries (16 points)) St. Helens, nil.

div.head: OLDHAM v. WIGAN.
div.p: OLDHAM v. WIGAN.

A run-away game was witnessed at Oldham, the home team running up the huge score of five goals eleven tries t 3 Wigan's nothing. Williams, Lees, Davies, Taylor, and Bonsor all crossed ths Wigan line, Lees kicking the goals. SWINTON v. BROUGHTON RANGERS.
The Rangers Fcored a lucky win, at Swinton, by one try to nil. Jackson registered the try in the op ening period.
YORKSHIRE SENIOR COMPETITION.
HOLBECK V. HALIFAX.
A win for Halifa.x by one goal and three tries to one try was the result of this game at Holbeck, Duke, Malt- house, 'Foothill and Riley played prominently. LEEDS PA.RISH CHURCH V. WAKEFIELD TRINITY.

The Church team at home were too strong for the Trinitarians, whom they defeated by four goals one try to nil. Fawcett—who kicked the goals—Howell, Lewis and Gill plavrd conspicuously for the winners. BATLEY V. BRIGHOUSE RANGERS.

The fifteens mot at Batley, where a close came was witneqsPd, the home side winning by two points to nil. The Batley forwards were mainly instrumental in their cluWs victory. BRADFORD v. HUDDERSFIELD'

This match at Park Avenue was well contested, Brad- ford being the victors by two goals two tries to one goal two tries. Roblrtson. Murgatroyd, and Cooper for Brad- ford,and Sutcliffe. Lorriman, and Williams for Hudders- field were the scorers. CASTLEFORD v. MANNINGHAM.

A one-sided game at Castleford resulted in a win for the home team by twenty-one points (all scored in the first half) to eight points, which were obtained by Man- ningham after the interval. LIVERSEDGE v. BRAMLEY.
Bramley had to admit 4ef9at at Liversedgl by the big margin of two goals and five trie; to nil, eleven of the points being scored in the first half. FIECSMONDWIKE v. RUNSLET.
In this match, at Heekmondwike, the visitors gained a wPII-meritei victory by two goals and one try to one goal. Hannah, A. Goldthorpe, and Bland scored for their respective sides.
LANCASHIRE "A" TEAMS CONIPENTION. WARRINGITON V. WIDNE3.

The Warringtdn "A "team representatives visited Widnes on Saturday in this competition. As matters stood, Warrington would have to defeat the Chemical men and Runcorn the following (next) week, lafore they could claim the champioAship medals. Much speculation and doubt was entertained as to the ultimate result of the game, for theugh Widnes was not consi- dered as good a team as they used to be they were de- tormined the medals should not be warn by the Warring- ton men if they could help it. The Widnesians' deter- mination was impelled by strong motives, though they themselves were not ire the running for the medals. Strangely enough, last year the position of affairs was just the reverse, for Widnes were competitors for the medals, and Warrington who had nothing at stake in the match defoated them decisively on Good Friday. Unfortunately, it was found at the last moment that Fish, who had been taken from the first team to play for the " A " team would be un- able to attend the match, and the hopes of the Warring- ton supportirs, who had been building on Ws appear- anc fell down to zero. There wer about 2,000 enthu- siastic spectators on the Widnes ground when the teams made their appearance, the composition Wing as fol- owe

- - Warrington : Boscow, full back; s,loeres. Duckwerth, Cross, Pendlebury, threequar`ers ; Aehurst and Allen, halves; Skelhorn, Tawnend, Deakin. Hatton. Cunning- ham, Jolley, Eden, Wilcocks,forwards. W:clnes : Percival, full back: Peacoak, Bawne, Tay- lor, Lomas, threeqearters ; O'Brien, Halligan, halves ; Redmond, Fos`er, Emery, Goulden, Wynne,.Thomas, Davies, Grace. forwards.. . Widnes started the game with the sun in their eyes,the visitors having the wind in their favour. Warrington were promptly ruled offside, and a few minutes later they were swarming round the Widnes uprights. Fine passing by the Widnes man took play back to half way. Bowne checked renewed pressure with a fine mark. Con- tinuing the pressure the Warrington men worked the ball up the field and Duckworth successfully dropped for goal. Bowne was promioent with some good play and a forward rush by the homesters was well checked by Boscow, Widnes knocking into touch. Eden made a gallant attempt to cross the line but speed failed him. Widnes beseiged the Warrington quarters for some time, but were enable to snore. Ashunr, was disabled and had to leave the field, the visitors playing one man short in consequence. Cross got possession and almost reached the line, but O'Brien stopped him. When the whistle sounded for half time the game was in favour of Warrington by two points to nil. It required a little d7scriminatien to see that now, Warrington was a beaten team. With the change of ends they had the wind against thorn and the sun in their eyes, and could only boast two points to the good. The play so far had only too conclusively proved, that if the visitor; were a better team in combination, yet the entire absence or speed amongst them, and pazticularly behind the pack, would be their downfall. The homesters were weak in their forward line but par- ticularly strong in the back division. Shortly after the re-commencement Aeharst pluckily entered the arena again, amid a general cheer. Widnes at once assumed the upper hand. Grace made a mark which gained some ground and Thomas scored with a free kick. The homesters did not attempt to play mu ‘h of a passing game but got in a mark at every opportunity and then punting strongly followed up giving Thomas.who played a capital game, every chance to drop for goal. The game continued in the home halt and Widnes getting a free kick Thomas landed the ball over the bar amidst deafening cheers. The same player dropped for goal a little later but just missed. Ashurst altered the game a little but only temporarily, play reverting to its old stage until Bowne taking a pass from a scrimmage grounded over the line,Thomas improving. The homes- ters were still pressing when "time" came with the re- sult: Widnes 3 goals, 1 try (9 points); Warrington 1 goal (2 points).

THE MUSICAL SOCIETY'S CONCERT.
MENDELSSWIN'S "ST. PAUL."

We are indebted to Mr. F. ll.Crossley, the con- ductor of the Warrington Musical Society, for the following notes on the subject of Mendelssohn's oratorio" St. Paul," which is announced for perfor- mance on Wednesday next. The rehearsals are, we believe, in an advanced and promising stage, and it will be seen from our advertisement columns that principal vocalists of high repute have been en- gaged. The society's orchestra will, as usual, be considerably amplified and a fine interpretation of the oratorio may be confidently looked forward to. In 1833 Mendelssohn accepted the post of musi- cal director at Dii3seldorf, and it was at this town that his first oratorio " St. Paul " was produced: Mendelssohn, when he first entertained the idea ef writing an oratorio, though he had not yet comple- ted his 23rd year, did not enter upon his task with- out consideration or without experience. He knew what an oratorio ought to be, for he had studied the old masters well, especially Sebastian Bach. But he was no imitator, he simply set to work upon Bach's principles, and afterwards worked out his own ideas in his own way. The words were com- piled by himself, and they were selected' with very few exceptions, from the German translation of the Bible. Three historical facts are presented in three distinct pictures,—the Martyrdom of St. Stephen, the conversion of St. Paul, and the Apostle's later career. A predominating influence throughout is the suggestion of the ultimate triumph of Christi- anity, and it is evidently in connection with this idea that Mendelssohn introduces so many chorales, for in Protestant Germany the chorale is univert— ally understood to represent the united Voice of the

whole Chfistian Church. In the first chorus "Lord, thou alone art God," the choral voices enter on mas- sive, sustained, forte chords led up to by a short crescendo passage in the orchestra. It is interest- ing to notice that Mendelssohn frequently repeats this device in his later works,—notably in the " Hymn of Praise" and "Elijah." The choruses throughout the work are of the utmost importance and variety, indeed they almost overshadow the solos, though there is at least one song for each voice of the vocal quartet of the highest degree of excellence; for the soprano the air "Jerusalem," for the contralto the arioso " But the Lord is mind- ful of His own," for the bass the scena "0 God have mercy upon me," and for the tenor the air "Be thou faithful unto death." Then the choruses. How ferociously real are the cries of the multitude at the stoning of Stephen and flow beautifully melodious is the funeral chorus "Happy and blest are they" when he is laid in the grave; while for breadth and power it would be difficult to name a more striking chorus than "0 great is the depth." The first performance of " St. Paul" took place at Diisseldorf in May 1836 under Mendelssohn's own direction, and four months later it was given for the first time in this country at Liverpool when it was conducted by Sir George Smart. The work sp,.edily became immensely popular and the num- ber of performances that took Oace all over Europe during the years 1837 and 1838 was quite extraor- fiinary.

div.p: THE ALLEGED SACRILEGE AT ST, ARTS ROMAN CATHOLIC CHURCH,
PRISONER COMMITTED TO THE SESSIO NS.

At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Friday. Daniel Davies was again brought up on remand charged With stealing from a charity contribution box at St. Mary's Roman Catholic Church, Buttermarket-street, on the 23rd February the sum of 4d. Mr. John Eckersley, baker, 25, Bridge-street, Warring- said on Thuusday afternoon of the day in question he went to the church to play the organ upstairs. He heard someone in the church and saw prisoner walk to the top of the church and then come down again. Witness heard a noise of money chinking and of a box breaking. Be went downstairs and saw prisoner standing some distance off the box which was close to the side door, and then make a sudden move towards the door. Witness then noticed the box was broken open. He called prisoner back and pointing to the broken box asked him if he knew anything about it. Prisoner said he bad not broken it open, he had money of his own. Witness took him across to the police station. To the best of his belief the box was all right when he went into the Church. Father Neville Wilson, priest at St. Mary's Roman Catholic Church, said he was in the church about 2 o'clock and did not notice anything wrong with the box. There would prcbably be not more than a few pence in it as it was emptied every Sunday. Prisoner Was an entire stranger to him. Mrs. Catherine Daley, wife of Thomas Daley, 37, Scotland-road. VarringtoO, said she was in the church about five minutes past three o'clock. .Sbe beard a 11°ise as if someone were walking on their toes and on turning round saw prisoner who dropped on one knee as though he winted to hide himself. Being frightened, Witness went across to the other side of the church and heard a noise of wood breaking. She was too terrified to turn round. She afterwards saw prisoner at the police Station and picked him out from amongst other men. Detective Superintendent Monaghan said be received the prisoner in custody, and found in his possession a screw driver (produced), a leather purse containing £3 in gold and 225. in silver and 7td. in copper. Witness returned to the Church and found the black box produced and the lid On the ' floor. He compared the impressions on the black box and an oak box not opened with the screw driver, and they corres- Ponded. He asked prisoner his name and address, and he replied "You rbust.find it out, I won't tell sou; my friends are respectable. and I don't want them to know Where I am." Witness afterwards cha4,ed him with stealing from the box, and be replied " I know nothing about it." The following day he gave the name of Daniel Davies. On Friday last wheb he was brought up on remand, prisoner spoke to witness and said "I am guilty of this job here; I only took 4d. out of the box, that's all there was in. That's God's truth !" That (Friday) morning witness chared him as he was now Charged, and he replied "Yes, it's right ; I took it."r Prisoner when asked what he had to say, said: " I Was under the influence of drink when I entered the Church, and as for the box, I do not remember any- thing about it. The magistratm committed him for trial at the next Liverpool Quarter Sessions.
