div.p: /Letters to the ttor.

NOTICE TO CORRESPONDENTS. Authors of letters intended for publication must in all cases send their names and addresses to the Editor. Matters intended for publication must be written on one side only of the paper. Correspondents are strongly advised to write briefly. A short letter has much greater chance of insertion than a long one.

WARRINGTON —CORPORATION BILL, Sir,—lf you will- allow 1119 space in your valuable paper, I should like to place before my fellow rite- payers a tew facts in connection with the Winalick Water Supply. In a eircular signed by the Mayor, it is stated that the well was originally constructed in 1878, to provide 600,000 gallons per 24 hours, and that the daily quintity pumped at the pr3sent time is 1,400,000 gallons. This is altogether misleading, We are not getting 1,400,000 gallons from a well constructed to provide 600,000 gal- lons, other wells have bsen sunk to obtain the present supply. Originally the wells were equipped with a pair of pumps capable of raising 700,488 gallons in 12 hours, after allowing 77,832 gallons for slip. Siace,other wells have been sunk, and another pair of pumps have been started, capable of raising 801,909 gallons in 12 hours, allowing 89,100 gallons for slip. Working the two pairs together, we have 1,502,388 gallans raised in 12 hours, which I think is about our present supply and has been for years. The Charts which were distributed last week., show an increase of about 9 per cent. from 1897 to 1898, in the consumption of Winwisk water, passing through meters; If we allow 10 per cent, on last year's coa- sumption, we shall have an average of 255,230 gallons per day passing through the meters, which, taken from the supply, leaves 1,247.158 gallons for domestic use. Taking the population of Warrington at 65,000, we have 19 gallons per day for every man, woman, and child. This for a family of 5 pirsons amounts to 95 gallons per day, or 665 gallons (18i barrels) per week. I have before me a statement, where, for a population of 57,146, the daily supply f'r domestic purposes, is 400,000 gallons, or 7 gallons per head. I think that 19 gallons per head, per day is an ample supply, and as there is no likelihood of this failing us, (seeing that we have parsed through a period, which holds a record for deficiency in rainfall and have not wanted), we have little fear of a water famine. Further, I assert that if the wells were put to the test, they would yield, from 50 to 70 per cent. more than they are doing, which would meet the growing demands for some years to come. Thanking you in anticipa- tion.—l remain, yours sincerely, G. L. BRIMELOW, 134, Manchester-road, Warrington.

div.head: NEWTON URBAN DISTRICT COUNCIL
div.p: NEWTON URBAN DISTRICT COUNCIL
ELECTIONS.
THE VIADI;Or WARD.

On Thursday evening a meeting was held in the Town Hall, Earlestown in support of the candidature of Mr. G. F. Clarke for the Viaduct Ward: :dr. J. G. Mullins presided, and there was a very fair attendance. The Chairman said he could not allow that op- portunity to pass without making reference to the ser- vices rendered by the candidate who was retiring, through ill-health, from the field. As ene who had al- ways taken an active part in his election, he had, as an elector of Viaduct Ward, to wi b that he would take with him into private life the consciousness of the fact, speaking personally. that he appreciited the services he had rendered to the township, and to the Viaduct Ward in particular, and he hoped that his life would be lone spared, and ;hat he might gain his former h alth, and be still able to reader service to the township. The time had again Come round when the choice of candidates to represent their interests on the Urban DisPriet Council for the Viadust Ward, must lea made. That meeting had been convened for the phrpose of promotine and furthering the candid %tare of Mr. G. F. Clarke, who, being a fellow townsman was well-known to all of them. Having been closely connected for some years with him, he ceuld speak with no uncertainty as to his business capacity and ability. His position in the world of finance justified more than words of his could convey, his ability for the position. Local self Govern- ment was an accomplished fact, and the object was that the Government of the people shoeld be by the people, and that it should be of the purest and best. He hoped in the conduct of this campaign nothing would be said on either side that should be personal. Mr. G. F. Clarke, the candidate, said he stood before them as a candidate desiring to represent their interests on the Urban District Council. He had had it put to him somewhat seriously that he was taking a very im- pulsive step and acting somewhat rashly in presuming to ask the electers of Viaduct Ward for support. An argument that had been put to him very strongly by a man who he would not for a moment think intended to do him any harm in tha meter, was the fact that he was in every way unworthy to represent the Viaduct Ward. The man was a working man, like himself, and he told him, the swelter, that his humble origin, and the watt he had been brought up and trained oueht to be a sufficient iadication to others that he was not worthy te represent the Viaduct Ward. Not only was thatempressed upon him in that way to disparage his efforts to represent them, but it was an attempt to cast a slur upo his parents. (Shame.) They knew all abets,: him, and in spite of inducements to remove else- where he hal decided to remain in the district where he had made so maav friends. If he was elected on the Urban District Council it would be his aim and en- deavour to represent their interests as faithfully as he possibly could. He knew his appearance in the Ward had caused a great deal of dissent, particularly amongst ee4ain sections, for what reason he did not know. He said the Viaduct Ward was not represented in a certain sense. H. did not think the electors of a Ward con- sidered the besiaess affairs of the Council in the light they ought to do,and the result was that those upon the Council looked upon their peaitions as sinecures,and any attempt at a contest caused a splutter of excitement. Until long after the 18th century a system of drain- age was never thought of, but the great cholera plague of 1847 led the authorities to consider the desirability of improving the sani- ation of the various townships throughout the country. The sanitation was the most important duty that an Urban District Council had to deal with. To-lay we were living in a much better stsee and condition than even o'er forefathers were, in those days, but we coeld not say that we had arrived at a system of perfection. There were two poirsts which he thought electors gener- ally bad lost sight of, he did not say that they Were not acquainted with them,balt it might be that they did not call to mind the powers that they had, if they were only ready'to exercise them. The Housing of the Working Classes Act of HO gave power to any four inhabitants of any district to call upon the Council to require a medical inspection of any property which they con- sidered of an insanitary cearacter. Then there was the Allotments Act. Any six ratepayers in any district might call upon the Urban District Council to provide allotments for them, and if the Council refused, they had a power of appeal to the County Council. These might , seem very trivial or unimportant matters but whether the powers be exercised or not the people should under- stand what the porters were, and at the same time that they were within thsir reach. He should adhere to the points in his address if elected to represent the Viaduct Ward, and he would go t e the Council in an indenead- ent manner, preparee to give an exereesion of his opinion without regard te the opinions of other members of the Council, Who might be lookine upon him or pass- ing glances tone to another. He should have an open mind upon any subject and try to let his opinion be in the best and truest interest* of the ratepayers of the t3weehip. If he was elected he should not famous any policy of extravay,ant expenditure, at the same time he did not believe in a false ecenomy. He thought that the business of the Council bath in sanitary and financial matters should be conducted nct only with regard to how m may could be saved, and the least that ctuld be spent. but what was hest in the interest of the people p both financially and in the public health of the town- ship. His opinion with regard to the public water supply was that the Ceuecil had taken a proper step in the matter when they contrived to get a supply that could not be controlled by any public company in the •district. He thought that it was a right and proper thing for every public authority to control its own water supply. He was in favour of proper working hours and a fair rats of wages f-or every capable employe of the Council. His declaration with regard to the huts on the Market ground had been variously received, bet he said that any person holding a hut on the Market ground should be tre tted in the same way as an ordinary trader.He thought the rent they paid should be equivalent to the same rent a pod shopkeeper should pay in the same locality. If they were to have competi:ion let them have it OR fair lines and let everyone have the same chance. He considered it was right that electors should hear an addrtss from their representatives on Council topics every 12 months. He was in favour of the Coun- cil meetings being held at six o'clock instead of four,and would vote for such a suggestion. Whatever the result of the election might be he meld only say that it would not affect him in any way, but if returned he Would en- deavour to represent their interests having due regard to the social and moral well being of the people, and sup- port every measure which he considered would be con- ducive to their welfare. " For the (mese that lacks assistance; For the wrong that needs resistance. For the future in the distance And all the good that I can do." That would be his aim. (Applause.) NEWTON DEBATING SOCIETY.

At the usual weekly meeting of this society, pre- sided over by Mr. T. E. Clough, the Rev. E. Bocock read a paper on" The position of women in reli- gion," in which he said that women were not suc- cessful as leaders. They served in some measure, to fan the flsme, but they failed as leaders. There was some discussion by the members, and theimeet- ing was most interesting. A RUNAWAY HORSB AT EARLESTOwN.

An incident which caused some excitement for the time being, happened in Earle-street on Wednes- day afternoon. A horse and trap was being driven over the bridge, which crosses the railway, leading from the Sugar Works, when the horse became alarmed at the noise made by Messrs. T. and T. Vicars buzzer" which was blowing, and bolted in the direction of Earle-street. It made straight for the shop window of Mr. Chorlton, tobacconist, but when everybody expected it would go through. it suddenly turned, and the shaft grazed the frame- work of the window,breaking the shaft and slightly damaging the window casing. Fortunately no further damage was done, and the horse was secured.

He would like to suggest that a great deal of time was always necessarily occu- pied in planning out any definite scheme for alteration of old buildings and it might be well to take time by the forelock te discuss what Macy would do with the old buildings when disused for their present purpose so that no time might be lost in doing what might be tetrad necessary and desirable. He was glad to think that the nursiaz staff was aeain c omplete. He regretted very much the necessity which the Local Government Board were under to refuse their assent to the appointment of the two nurses selected but he believed he was right in saying that the refusal was justified by subsequent events. He was sorry to h3ar thatinfluenzo had attacked some of the Board's officials, and necessarily, he was afraid, a good deal of inconvenience would result. Re- ference had been made that morning to the Brabazen scheme and he was glad to bear it was going on successfully. It was a scheme, which if kept within proper limits was very desirable, but there was the danger to which reference was made that it might be introduced somewhat to the extinction of work being done for the workhouse which would other- wise be deco. That was being guarded against at War- rington and that being so they must look, not to the financial results so much as to the occupation which was given to old people who would not otherwise have anything to do with their fineers and who thereby were relieved from the tedium of their existence in the work- house. There had been coins correspondence with re- ference to allewine Roman Catholic inmates under class D to leave the house for the purpose of attending mass. The Beard, he thought, had done everything they could in the matter, and he thought they had acted very liberally in making provision for the spiritual wants of the inmates, aid particularly those who did not belong to the Established Ceurch. Those effe:ts were fully acknowledged in the correspond- ence which had taken place. He might mention that since the Local Gevernmeet Board cemmunicateci with the Board of Guardians another letter had been receive I fronelthe Catholic Society in which they fully acknow- ledged the efforts made by the Board of Guardians to meet their wishes. (Hear, bear.) They again pro- posed that those in class D should not be debarred from going out on Sundays. He could quite see that to allow these people to go out without restrictions would probably lead to results that the Board was anxious to avoid. Perhaps a system might be found by the adoption of the issuing of tickets which had worked with good results in some unions. When a person was allowed to go out at the Workhouse he was given a ticket showing the time he left and that was signed by the priest at th chapel at which he attended Showing that he hod attended service there. He thought something of that kind might be UV- fut. Of course it would be necessary to be very strict as to the time of returning after the service. The per- son under those circumstances must come straight back from chapel. If enyteing of that kind could be done it would be a good thing, at any rate as an experime et. He was SUM the-members did not wish to debar these in- mates from any worship they might wish to attired. Merely as an experiment it could ,be tried, and it could be stepped at any moment if it Were found to work un- sati factorily. 113 saw the Board was entertaining the idea of intreiducine electricity, and the comfort and pleasure of eleetricity was very great. He hoped the Board would be able to make satisfactory arrangements for its introduction. (Hear, hear.) The CHAIRMAN said the subjects referred to by Mr. Jenner Fast would be attended to by the several com- mittees. The Board certainly did not like preventing any of the inmates from going to church bet still the charantere of those who had been prevented were such as to prevent the Botrd from seeing their way clear to allow them out of toe house. The matter, however, would have further consideration. The Board was very much obliged to Mr. Fast for his suggestions, and he hoped they might have Some good results. (Hear, hear). Mr. A. J. JOLLEY said he was very pleased to hear Mr. ITtent's statement with reference to the treatment of the inmates respecting their religious opinions. The Board !eel the facts of the case very clearly before the Local Government Board, and although the number of people affected by the classification rule was very small, it might inflict a hardship which the Board did not desire to inflict. He would submit a reso- lution which would cover the ease and enable the House Cemmitt.e to deal with the matter. The resolution was as follows That the gouge Com- mittee be empowered to suspend their rule preventing Roman Catholic inmates in class D attending mass, and if thoug t desirable, to allow particular inmates under saitable precautions to leave the Workhouse temporarily for that purpose only." With regard te the tickets he (Mr.Jolley) might say that they used to be in use. He be- lieved the reason why they were dropped was that it was too much trouble for the priests to sign them. But the nuntb,r of people in CIVIS D was so small that there would not be much difficulty now. He found that out of 161 inmates,there were only six affected by the rule. The Board Was qui e prenered to deal as reasonably as it could with the Catholic inmates. Mr. DAVIES seconded and the resolution was unani- mously carried. ACCEPTANCE OF TENDER 3.

COLONEL PILKINGTON Kr.

Parr Hall was crowded on Tuesday evening, on the occasion of a Unionist meeting held under the auspices of the Warrington Conservative Association. Mr. J. Charlton P or, J.P.. C.C., presided, and he was sup- ported be Lord kshbourne (Lord Chancellor of Ireland), Mr. R. Pierpoint, M P. Colonel Pilkingten, M P, Sir Gil- bert Greentll Bart, John White, Alderman Sutton, Alderman Hutchioson, Ceuncillors Heaton, Shillcock, Smethurst, Longton, Dr Seerratt, and Messrs C S Bar- gees, W Bloomfield, le Isherwood, R Parr, W Holbrook. W.l Forshaw, B Griinthaw, R Johnson, T S Steele, V Davies, W H M .akin, A J Willett, R Ibleson,J E Seeker, G Pilling, E Bradshaw, W J Sea w, II Tibsley, S Oven, J Houghton, W Owen' T H Pdkington, and others. The CII&IRSIfiN said he could not help thinking that it might be in part owing to their old Coneervative re- cord that they had—if he might so express it—won a gold medal from the heads of the party that had induced the Lori Chancellor of Ireland to come amongst them that night. (Applause.) lie would also extend, both on his own and their part, a very hearty welcome eci their friend Colonel Pilkingtqn. (Applause.) That was his first public appearance in Parr Hall, Warrington. Be had come' as he need not remind them, after a very bloodless victory in a neighbouriag constituency. Long might he hold the undispu ad membership of the New- ton Division of Lancashire. (App ause.) Be would like to t ake that opportunity of reminding their friend L nrd Ashbourue that close his last visit—and he would alinest say pos iibly one of the outcomes of it—a. Junior Conser- vative Association had been formed in Warrington. (Ap- plause.) It had induced the young Conservatives of the party to take an interest in politics. They had already done good service to the oil asso- ciation, and hid given evidence of strength and vitality, and he was quite sure they were ready when the time came to take their places in the foremost ranks of the battle, to win their spurs, and to show that l'hey were made of the same stuff that had gained so many triumphs in the old days in Werrineton. (Applause). The Soudan had been restored to Eeypt, and the English flag was flying over Khartoum, and a college had just been established in °rein. to perpetuate the victory of civilization over barb trianism, of light over darkness, and all this he believed had been accom- plished in consequence of their having a strong Govern- ment at home, presided over by a great and powerful Minister—Lord Salisbury. (Applause.) With a Cabinet of able and energetic men, and not least a strong and determined public opinion behind them,all this had been accomplished, and the whole world had looked on, and they had gained respect, and it had given confidence in England and produced prosperity. the outcome of con- fidence and good trade. (A splause.) He also believed that it had strengthened the bonds of union between Britain and Greater Britain ; that it had broueht the English people nearer together, and that they were hand in hand throughout the world for the maintenance of peece, justice, and liberty. (App!aute). Colonel PILKINGTON, M.P., moved the following reso- lution :—"This aiming desires t 3 record its high enure- cietion of the manner in which Lord Salisbury and Her Makesty'a Government have conducted the affairs of the empire during their tenure of office' the results of their policy being profound peace abroad and great develop- ment of trade at home" When they came to consider what the position of affairs was some three or fear years ago, when the p-esend Government took office, he , thought they realised the truth of the resolution, and the strong contrast between the present and the past. It was changed because they sent a party to power in 1835 that was determined on two or three things. The first thing that they made up their mind to do was to establish the United King loin in a strong and firm position with reference to other nations. , (Applause.) Bound up, of course, with that was the q eeetion of trade. When the Unionist Government was returned to power, and when the Cabinet was formed, the first thing to be done was to complete and extend in every possible way the defences of the ceuntry—the army and navy. The Government were perfectly cee- tain that if they did that the trade of the country would settle down, capitalists would have confidence, and workingmen would find that capital being certain their wages would bec nne cirtain too. During the last three or four years every effort had been made to pet the navy in such a position that the United Kingdom, her celonies,and the trade of the country would be safe. In consequence of that policy the first Lord of the Admirs alty,Mr.Goschen—(aoplause)—was able to tell the House that whereas in 1895 they had something like 80,000 sailors,irew the had something like 110,000. (Applause.) The Government had established a solid peace, because they were now respected and understood, and their position wae'clear before all the nations of Europe. (Ap- plause.) They were still carrying on this great work of perfecting the defences of the country, because although the navy was very strong, there were manylhings that required attention. They wanted a great many more swift cruisers that would be sufficiently powerful and sufficiently speedy to overtake the cruisers, some of the other nations were thinking of building, in order that if anything did happen to this country they would be able to attack not only their navy but their commerce. The army WA3 being equipped in proportion to the other armies, and it would take some months before they actually completed it. But when that was done there Would be a further step to be taken with regard to the militia and volunteers. These required to be equipped with a proper force of artillery and cavalry, but that, of course, would be a matter for the future. (Applause.) Be felt quite sure that in 18 months they would again send to power for another six or seven years the party that now for 12 years had done suels splendid service for the country. (Applause.) Alderman SUTTON seconded the resolution, which was unanimously carried. Lard ASHBOURNE, who had a hearty reception. said the Government of the day was marked not unfairly for criticism, for attack, and for assault, and if they had been tried by every fair standard they had been fairly able to stand the measure of criticism directed against them—(voises : "You have." "No," and ap- plause)—and they were a united Government and a united Cabinet. ("No," "yes," and applause.) But at all events he was entitled to speak upon that subject with an authority that no" no" could silence. (Cheers.) Allow him to say that he never shrank from addressing opponentt,but he hoped that opponents when they came to their meetings would be witling to listen to what they had to say. (Applause.) The Unionist party were not only sustained by a united Cabinet, but also loyally supported by a great party. They were willing to be judged by their friends as well as by their enemies, by thoughtful intelligent public opinion. (Cheers.) Now their opponents were entitled te be spoken of with re- spect, and most certainly with sympathy. (Laughter.) Lately one of their most distinguishsel men—Sir Edward Grey—for whom everyone must entertain unalloyed re- spect for the patriotism and public spirit with which he applied himself to the great topics which -came before the House of Cornmens he said that adversity was 'the isest discoverer of virtue. Ha (Lerd Ashbourne) dared say it was. (Laughter.) Un- questionably their opponents had a great deal of ad- versity, quite enough to entitle them to find a gned deal lof virtue. (Lauehter.) Let them hope as time went on, although their adversity might continue, their virtues might inerea,se. (Laughter and applause.) They had been unfortunate in having to submit to changes in their leaders, of whom again he desired to speak with the respect which he sincerely felt for them. Lord Rose- bery. a man of ability in many walks of public life, thought it w:se and prudent to resign his difficult, ard- uous, and thankless position. It was not for him (the speaker) to presume to pees judgment upon his action, but his private opinion was that he was right. That was quite private. (Laughter.) Sir William Harcourt, leader in the House of Commons, a man of unrivalled House of Commons' experience, most rightly acknow- ledged to be a man of great ability, of splendid courage and great resource, deemed it who and prudent and sensible to resign. It was not for him (the speaker) to criticize his action, or its wisdom, or the grounds upon which he acted. Having given his private opinion with reference to Lord Rosehery's action,he was not disposed te say that he had a different eVnion in reference to what Sir William Harcourt had dense (Laughter.) Some parties were not very easy to lead. They did not know who they -'ere leading. They did not know who was following. They did not know what they were leading them to. (Laughter.) But a new leader had been lately elected for the House of Commons a gentleman whom they all respected, and whom it was impossible not to like, an agreeable, attractive, able and experienced member of the House of Commons, Sir H. Campbell-Bannerman. He wished him every prosperity in his difficult tack. (Leuehter.) It was not a desirable thing for a Government that an Oppesitinn should not be strong. It was a great deal better for the public life of the country to have a clearly-clefined vigorously- led Opposition. Sir H Campbell-Bennerman bad a difficult task, which he was sure he would encleseentir to discharge with great shill and ability. Sir H. Campbell-Bannerman would have to deal with the question of Home Rule. They were all familiar with that question. His difficulty was that he knew that Nationalist members from Ireland had certain clear ex- pectations upon that subject, and he would find it herd to remain in touch with them and net to lose entire touch with English public opinion. (Applause.) He did not care how clever a man was, that was an ex- tremPlv diffienit noaitinn, b.na.nga he wen'd ha V. Po

satisfy two sets of opinion entirely different in character He would have to try to please the Irish Nationalist mem- bers and else please the Enelish Liberal coostituents who were thoroughly tired of the question. What the Liberal leader suggested was teat he loved Home Rule and believed in it. It was one of the dearest and most earnest wishes of his life, inscribed upoa his heart, but they could not expect that he ceuld off-hand give effect to it—he had such a lot of interests to consider before he could take it on. (Laughter.) He named four: Circumstances of time (General Election), the feeling c,f the nation, the temper of the party, and, before everything, the quality and quantity of the majority. (Laughter). And he passed from the question with the statement that they would be true to the Irish people as lone as they were true te themselves. What on earth did that mean ? (Laugh- ter). It was a sentence which, pronounced by a con- scientious man in a conscieatioue manner to an enthu- siastic audience, was sure to be cheered, but what in the living world it meant no human being could tell. (Laughter.) He would leave the subject with the remark that if theLiberel party by any chance did get a majoety and went into pewer,his acute and ready fellow ceuntrymen, with all tee insistence of the Irish nature and all the keenness of determination to get what they asked for, would press him until this question was la:ought. forward into a position of prominence. There was another question which the Liberals discussel, and he invited their attention to the way in which it was discussed. It was, in fact, not discussed. It was men- tioned and ran away from. (Laughter.) He referred to the question of the Sudan, and what had been done the-e. (Applause.) It was a page in English history which they had a right to be proud of, that a great tract of the world's surface in a state of barbarism, horribly mis-ruled, had, ins the interest of civilization and humenity,in the interest combined of England and Egypt. been rescued from its horrible condition, and England found then as at all times in her history, that she had a man ready to fulfil the greatest task that could be placed upon a man's shoulders. (Applause) In China our sphere of influence WAS wider acd mere clearly defined than it had ever been before in the his- tory of that country. E ogland wanted no more territory but only an outlet for her trade and her civilising influ- ence. Ties Government's efforts ha the matter of Chins had been eteadsly directed to the wotection and develop- ment, of E aghse commerce. Let the position of Eigland amongst the nations of the world to-day be contrasted with what it was three yea's ago. Wauld any mac will an imagination or a Meet•ore, deny that. England stood higher and stronger now than it did then? He had only to instance our relations now as compared to what they were thon with America, wits Russia, and with Ger- many. From Ballet& there had recently come the Tsar's inyitreon to a disarmetnent conference. It was impossible not to speak of that i svitatioa in terms of the heariest and most genuine sympathy. It was a splendid conception, but until other Powers consented to disarm England must continue to be nreotred for contineeaciss. He was happy in having been oe personal and excellent terms with his oopenents—(applause)—eni he thought he had done come little in promoting the good feeling between his opponents and himself. Referring to a correspondent who had written saying that his (Mr. Pierpnint's) same hid not appeared in the division lists this session, the speaker, said he ventured to state, and Lori Ash- bourne would bear him out that a member of Parliament who stayed at the end of a session was infinitely more useful than a man who turned up at the commence- ment of the session. When speaking of policy the proof of the pudding was in the eating. He suggested that they shou'd wait until the whole of the cooking was done before they said anything about it. The aver age attendance of members at the last session was 791 in the division list. His attendance reached 145, which was higher than any one of his neighbours. (A.pplauee.) Taking the whole Parliament from its beginning in 1895 up to the end of last session for the same gentlemen the average would have been 354 ' 1-6. The member for Warrington had made 504. (Applause.) The directors themselves evidently do not re- gard their dutiee as limited to the attainment of security for the policy holders and profit of the shareholders. As Mr. Horne said at the 50th annual meeting, they aie keenly alive to their public resnensibilitiee. A company Iwhinh insures the lives of one third of the population is practically a national institution, and it cannot be cerriei on without sympathetic response to the vibrations of popular sentiment and national thought. An aspect of the company's work which is rather public than private is brought into prominence by the share which iP always tike in'relleving the distress occasioned by Mei aceidents in different parts of the world. Thus of the 34 lives lost when the Albin was launched, 16 were insured with the company. On all these occasinns the omninntent Prudential seems to be hover- ing round with such consolation as it; constitution per- mits it to give to the relatives of the lost. Turning to the consideration of the years busieees proper, we find in every line of the report evidence of healthy growth and exnberant activity. William James Glover and Co., have carried on a steadily increasing business for the last 80 years, making wires and wire ropes of all kinds; like most family concerns, their business has now outgrown their capital hence the present offer to the public. The company has also acquired a large and well- situated factory in Warrington to carry on the manufacture of electric wires and cables; this business is probably the most lucrative industry of the nresent day; the demand for electric cables hav- ing increased quite fourfold during the last four years, in fact it is keener now than ever it was, in spite of the high price of copp Ir, and the time of year, this being the slack season. In connection with electric cablemaking, the Company has also taken over a mechanical rubber concern, which will enable them to effect a considerable saving in cost of raw materials. The profits of the Electrical Cable Department alone are fully expected to reach 25 per cent. and the actual net certified pro- fits made by Messrs. Glover and Co., and the Mechanical Rubber Department, have been already sufficient to pay the interest on the Preference Shares. The assets of the Company exclusive of goodwill and patents will amount to £67,328 6s 01., and there,/ will be a working capital of £33,000. GARLAND, Bridge-st., Warrington. SPIDIMS AND THEIR HABITS."

This was the subject of a very interesting lantern lecture by Mr. Liu. Greening delivered before the members of the Wycliffe Young People's Society on Monday evening. At the outset the lectnrer re- ferred to the spider's place in nature and to the relations of spiders, the distinctive differences be- ing clearly shown. The numerous varieties of spiders were described,and by a number of interest- ing slides the audience was enabled to watch the growth of the spider from the egg, showing its transformations during the twenty-one days of in- cubation. The anatomy of the spider was faith- fully porrayed, and special attention was directed to the spinneret by which the spider was enabled to spin its web. One of the most interesting por- tions of the lecture was that in which the habits and nests of spiders were dealt with, showing a considerable amount of intelligence on the part of these wonderful creatures. The habits of the water spider were especially interesting and Mr. Greening pointed out that the only place where they could be found in this district was in Arpley fields. The slides were shown on the screen by Mr. Knowles, secretary of the Photographic Society. At the close of the lecture, Mr. Greening Was heartily thanked for his services on the motion of Mr. B. Hall seconded by Mr. Witts. Mr. Greening in ack- nowledging the compliment advised young men to take up the study of natural history and assured them that they would find it both interesting and profitable. A. vote of thanks to Mr. Wyllie for pre- siding, closed the meeting.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.

RUGBY FOO NALL. The condition of things in Warrington football circles is going from btl to wfirst., and only one more blow can fall—and that is that Wirrinvon should be knocked out of the cup-ti,s in the firer round. I am not so despon- dent as to anticipate th:s yet, hut the events of Saturday were very nearly proving toe last straw. Our lack of confidence in the pr 'wen of the first team was such that a defeat from Widnes wig confidently, almost cheerfully expect:A. and yei 3 got it, but there was some hope that the " A " team would succeed in capturing the meials. They also failed however, and the disap- pointment was intenle in Warrington on Saturday even- ing, when the news bectme known. Mingled with the disappointma at were feelings nf resentment with the csornittee for the way in which they had mismanaged matters.

I fortnight ago the "A " team 3oemei certain of topping th," A" teams' Lague, until a c9rtain club located at R ochrl Ile checked their progress. It was here that the committee started their stries of blunders. They were fully aware that there was only slight chance of winning at W.dhe i,and th-7 ought to have thrown their energies ireo making certain of two points at W:cticiale. Instead of doing so they sent th 3 ordinary team, which got licked, and then of cour4o the committee took fright,and tried to recover everything at the last minute. If they meant to put first team men on the" A" team, why on earth did they not do it in time? I don't ap- prove of this method of winging the championship, and it is only justified when (Amer chios do the same, but if they mean to do it the committee should do it at the right time. A. win at Rochdale would have made the chamoionship practically certain, for the Widnes match could have been lost without affecting the result. How- ever, 'tis little use crying over spilt milk.

There is another way of looking at the matter too. The committee got their deserts oe Saturday, though it was at the cap also of the "'A "team lads. Last year they played" Smack "Bats againss Widnes " A" when the latter were badly ire need of a couple of points, an I de- feated them as a matter of cons?. This unsportsman- like act has never be In forgiven in Widnes, and the " Chemicals " had ample revenge on Saturday. The Warrington " A "team was met with taunts in every direction, both from players and spectators alike, and it was quite plain to them that the home team meant to win by fair means or foul. Wish such bitter feeling shown the!odds against Warrington were deubled, and in the end they hal to knuckle uoder. They thus owe their loss of the medals solely to the committee, and par- ticularly to the individnals who were 133 ill-advised as to play B Lte against Widnes "A "last year. I am very sorry for the" " team players. They have fought rnalfully for the trophy all through the season, and it is evreusely hard luck to be robbed on the line, as it were. It is a bitter disappeintment to them, but they most not despair. With their defeat Warrington's last hope of redeeming the season from total failure has al- most gone. There is -lust one chanee left—in the cup- ties—and wa all know how perilously slender that chance is.

The following paragraph made bitter reading in Mon. day's " Athletic News " :—" If S alforrs first fiftsea have fallen to pieces, the second team have upheld the great and glgeous reputation of the Royal borough. They have performel with a consistency which com- mands admiration, and on Saturday had the pleasure of hearing of the defeat of Warrington "A," a result which gave the New Barns janitors the championship of the division. They will rlc 'iv° gold medals for the notable achievement."—The "Salford Juniors" ought to think themselves lucky. But for the good turn which Jack Frost did them they would still be behiad Warrington In the race for the modals.

Andnow for the pramier team,whom Widnes whopped by 16 points to 3. By their curious actions the com- mittee succeedat in making both teams as weak as pos- sible on Saturday, ani the result was disaster. The fir t t ant, minus Bate, Ashurst, Fish, Boardman and S3holtze had not the ghost of a chance against the all- conquering Widnesians. The latter came to Wildsrspool with one hand on the cup, and they got a firmer grip on that desirable•article before they returned. With a full team on they made m;ncemeat of the Warringtonians, and af ;er a defensive first_half against the wind and sun, they rubbed it in warmly. A couple of tries were scored and three goals added to the couple dropped before the interval. Not since the match at Oldham have I seen Warrington so hopelessly at sea, so painfully beaten, as they were in the second half against Widnes. Neither forwards nor backs could make the slightest headway.

For the first twenty minutes Warrington really look,d as if they were going to s2cure a lead which would take some reducing. Th4y played a dashing game, found Batey completely off, and registered a try by Taylor. With Bate in his usual place it is very probable that they would have got in a time or two, hut without him their eff3rts were very crude. Widnes held a decided superior- ity forward and in two visits to the Warrington end they secured a couple of dropped goals, with which fled all Warrington's hopes, On crossing over Widnes held a lead of one point, and the match was virtually over. As I have already indicated Warrington were simply run off their feet in the second half, and must have been glad when the finish came.

There was only one satisfacbry feature about the match, and that was the size of the crowd. It is months since the enclosure was packed all round, and the" gate" on Saturday was one of the best—if net the best—this seasnn. The beautiful day, the successes of the visitors, and the nresence in their ranks of twa Warriogton lads, J. Hu.gies and E. Hughes all combined to make the fixtura an interesting one. It was clear proof of the way a winning team is supported,to see the crowds of followers accompanying the Widnes fifteen. J. Hughes, the threequarter, created a very favourable impression in the minds of the War. rington erowl,and there were many who wished he had int been allowed to slip into the clutchee of the Widnes club. For such a youth he played pluckily, was neat in all he did, and showed a promising turn of speed. It is probable that Warringtm will have cause to regret deeply their slowness in missing young Hughes. There is some talk of another Warrington lad going the same way. Let the committes of the Warrington Football Club take warning and be on the alert this time.

Though Widnes are such a strong team this year, I am not favourably impressed with the capabilities of their backs. Excepting Batey, they are an average lot, prominent only with resolute tackling. Occasionally they combine well,but they are far from being "classy. 'Batey played a poor ganv on Stturday all through, though there is no minimising the itiltll.l.l9B service his huge punts, and goal ki!kirig prlwrss, were to the winners in the second half. H dram quite failed to deal with the work thrown on him, and des not get rid of the ball anything like so well as he did a shlrt time ago. Isher- wood. Harris, and W:lclx all played well for Warrington hut Wood in particular was very weak in the centre. He is a long way off being fit for the first team yet. Be- tween the two sets of forwards there was a vast differ- ence. The Wilials eit;ht were far stronger and speedier than the home players, and fully upheld their reputa- tion for dash. On Saturday's form there was a palp- able weakness in every section of the Warrington team.

A word for Mr. S. Willian4. the refElre3. He was a strikiny exampl,4 of general incompetence on this occa- sion. Perhaps hq was off-colour, or his whistle was twisted. At all events it sounded on some odd ocea- si,os, for sornl nflrilr ni.aglng, and was mute for no reason at all on other occaslons.

The Company has taken over .Mr. G. R. Heyl-Dia's English Patent, No. 2610/99, and the processes connected there- with, for the insulation of Electric Light Cable with a kind of paper specially manufactured for the purpose. This material consists of a cellulose substance which will be impregnated with an insulating medium during the process of being made into sheet or strip. Further expensive and unrelable impregnation of the covered cables, as now carried on by other cable manufactures, will be avoided. The Cables wi I be also less rffected by heat. The Company will manufacture the following classes of Cable :- 1. India-Rubber covered Wires and Cables. For House Installation's, Mining, and Shipwork. The India-Rubber Compounds used by the Company are manufactured according to strictly chemical and scientific principles in their own works, so that ddterioration of the Rubber will be avoided. 2. Flexibles, Cotton Covered Wires and Cables. For Dynamo Builders, Inside Installations, and Transformer- makers, 3. Heyl Dia's Patent Cellulose-Silicate Electric Light Cables. For Corperation Electricity Mains, hlectric Tramways, and Railway Companies. &c. 4. Dry Core Underground Taephone Cables. For Munici- palities. Telephone Companies, Post Office, and (*overn- ment Offices. 5. Lead Covered Cables of every description. lICCKEY. --- ALTRINCHAM v. LATCHFORD. Played at Bowdon. in lovely weather. The game throughout was decidedly in AltrinchP m's favour, and it seemed they would win with a big score, but Latch- ford brought a capital goalkeeper, who repulsed the Altrincham forwards and baffled them many times. Goals were scored by E. Chorlton (two), Lambert (two), L. Brown, and Brewer. Final result :—Aitrincham, six goals; Latchford, nil. , STOCK TON HEATH v. MACCLESFIELD. At Warrington in glorious weather. Neither club was fully represented. With sun and wind in their favour 'Macclesfield pressed continuously in the first half, and ed by three goals to none at the interval. The home team attacked on resuming, and scored tvrice,by Gandy and Woods. The visitor 3 pulled themselves together, however, and Hope and H. Goodwin put through on their behalf before the clo3e. Result !--Macclesfield ye goals; Stockton Heath, two.

LADIES AND GENTLEMEN, Having been invited by a large number of prominent ratepayers, principally Workingmen (who think that a little new blood should be infused into the District Council's proceeding 3), to come forward in t'aeir interests as a Work- ingman's Candidate, it is with pleasure that I do so. I do not contest the seat on political or religious grounds, but simply and solely in the interests of the Working Classes and for the purpose of upholding and watching their requirements. As a Workingman and one well known to you, I feel that I can with confidence appeal to you for support, and if elected my endeavour will always be to keep down the rates. My interests are your interests, and what affects rue effects you. As one well acquainted with the wants of the Bridgewater Ward having resided in it for a number of years, you may depend upon it I shall spare no pains in serving your interests faithfully and well. Your obedient Eervant. WILLIAM SHAW, Jun. Top Locks, 11,mcorn.

A sensational affair materiel in Cardiff on Wednesday night.—The body of a missing woman, Margaret Caved!, was recovered from the Ely river soon awe two o'clock. The throat had been cut in several places, but otherwise the body bore no marks of violence. Tne prisoner, °aeries John Caveill; her husband, was subsequently charged with murder, and will be charged before the magistrates to-morrow morning. TEN ATLANTIC STEAMERS GIVEN UP AS LOST. Miss Reed,a pupil of the City of London Lying-in-Hos- pital, delivered a poor woman named Cheese, living at Sarah's Buildings, Old-street, London, of four infants, three girls and one boy, the last, a girl, being still-born.
